activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Code-switching is moving between two languages within one conversation; it is common among fluent bilinguals and is not by itself a sign of weak skill.
story:
Raphael had commandeered the kitchen table by six, spreading notecards from the fruit bowl to the stove, and by seven his mother had stopped pretending she could make tea around him. The assignment was printed in Ms. Morales's tidy hand: five minutes, entirely in French, on whether university education should be free. "Entirement en français," the sheet said twice, underlined, as if she had already imagined them trying to cheat.

He had the argument. That was the insult of it. He could write the essay in his sleep, could have defended either side in English with references and a joke at the end. Free tuition was munificent in principle, a gift the state extended to the young, but someone had to pay the lecturers, and in his draft he'd quoted a statistic about graduate taxes. In French, all of it dissolved. The vocabulary he reached for slid away at exactly the moment pressure arrived, and what came out instead was a hybrid thing, half one language, half the other, like a bridge that ends in water.

"L'éducation supérieure devrait être... should be free because," he said to the kettle, and stopped, and put his forehead on the table. The notecards smelled of the marker he'd used, sharp and chemical. Outside, a neighbour's sprinkler ticked against the fence.

Cassandre arrived at eight with her own cards and a bag of bread she set down without ceremony. She was doing the same debate, opposite side, and they had agreed to be each other's audience. She sat, took a bite of bread, and said, "Go. From the top. Five minutes, I'm timing."

He got forty seconds in before the first slip, and she raised one finger without looking up. He got another minute before the second, and she raised two. "It's not that I don't know it," he said, dropping into English, and she raised three fingers, which he understood to mean that even the complaint counted.

"I slip when I'm arguing," he said, in French, slowly, choosing each word like a stone he had to carry across a river. "When I care."

Cassandre put down the bread. Her older sister taught at a school in Marseille, she said, where the kids moved between French and Arabic inside a single sentence, sometimes inside a single clause, and nobody there thought it meant they were weak in either. There was a word for it, she said. "Code-switching." She shrugged, as if the word were a small thing she was handing over, and told him the sister's students did it most when they were thinking hardest, not least.

Raphael turned that over while the sprinkler ticked. He had been treating the slips as leaks, holes in a hull he had to patch before the debate, and Ms. Morales's double underline had agreed with him. But if the switching came at the pressure points, then the pressure was the problem, not the language. He could not argue in French yet the way he argued in English, fluid and armed, because he had not yet argued in French at all. He had only recited. Reciting was safe and useless. The slips were where the real thinking broke through, thinking too fast for his second vocabulary, and the answer was not to slow the thinking but to speed up the vocabulary until they matched.

So he tried it her sister's way, on purpose. He argued the free-tuition case at full speed and let the English words fall in where they fell, not apologising, not stopping, using them like borrowings, like tools left on the table. "The state est généreux, but generosity... la générosité costs," he said, and found that each English word showed him the French one he'd been groping for, the way a wrong answer can show you the shape of the right one. Cassandre timed it. Three minutes, then four, then the timer on her phone chimed and he was still standing, still talking, and the argument had never once stopped moving.

He spent the next hour doing it again, then again, and each time the English intruded less, not because he had forbidden it but because he had stopped being afraid of it. By eleven the kitchen smelled of marker and bread and the cold tea his mother had never made. He still didn't know whether entirely in French meant entirely, in Ms. Morales's mind, or whether five clean minutes were possible for him by Thursday, and he decided, stacking the cards, that he would aim for clean and not be ashamed of whatever surfaced. He put the cards in his bag, turned off the kitchen light, and in the dark hallway he heard himself say, quietly, "Bonne nuit," and then, after a pause, "see you tomorrow."

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: On a closed interval, a function's largest value can occur at an endpoint where the derivative is not zero, so the endpoints must be checked as well.
story:
Sara took her quiz out of her backpack and smoothed it on the counter between the slurpee machine and the lottery scratch cards, next to the register where Tate was counting out change for a bag of chips. Mr. Crowchild, who owned the corner store and had retired from teaching math before she was born, leaned over from his stool. There was a red circle around her answer on the last question, and beside it he had written, in the same red, three over ten.

"Find the maximum of f of x equals x cubed minus three x on the interval from negative two to two," Sara read aloud. "I found where the derivative is zero. That's what you do. The derivative is three x squared minus three, so x is one or x is negative one, and the biggest value is two, at both of them." She slid the paper toward him. "He circled the two and wrote a question mark."

Mr. Crowchild picked up a pen from beside the register, the kind with the chewed cap, and turned the quiz over to the blank back. "Tell me what the function does at the ends," he said.

"There's nothing at the ends. The derivative is zero at one and negative one, that's where the max is."

"Is it?"

Tate came around the counter with the chips open already, scattering salt on the glass. She looked at the back of the quiz upside down. "You got a six?" she said. "You got a hundred on the last one."

"The last one was an open domain," Sara said. "This one has a closed interval." She said the word interval the way her teacher had said it, like a boundary fence. She was starting to feel the shape of what she had missed, though not its contents yet, the way you can feel rain before you can name the cloud.

Mr. Crowchild drew a wobbly pair of axes on the paper. "Sketch it," he said, and stood up to serve a woman buying milk and a newspaper, leaving Sara alone with the pen. She plotted a few points, the numbers turbid in her head until they came out on the page, one at a time, and became clear. At x equals one the value was negative two. At x equals negative one it was two. Then, because he had asked, she tried the endpoints. At x equals two, the function was two. The same as her maximum. And at x equals negative two, it came out to negative two, which was the same as her minimum at x equals one. She sat back. "It's a tie," she said. "At negative one and at two."

"Equal," Mr Crowchild said, counting out the milk change. "So is the maximum at the critical point, or isn't it?"

"It's at both. But it also happens at the endpoint, where the derivative isn't zero at all." She checked the derivative at two, the arithmetic quick in her hand now: three times four minus three is nine. Nine, not zero. The function was still climbing when the interval cut it off. "I only checked the places where the derivative was zero. The function can keep going right past its critical point and hit its biggest value at the edge instead." She looked at the red question mark. "He never said that in class. Or he did and I wrote down only half of it, the half I already understood."

Mr. Crowchild took the pen back and added a small vertical bracket at each end of her sketch, closing the curve off. "Your teacher postulates nothing when he marks you wrong," he said. "He just checks the ends." Tate laughed around a mouthful of chips. Sara copied the corrected work onto a fresh page, then a second page, testing the ends of every interval until it stopped being something she remembered and started being something she did. Somewhere in the third example the habit began to calcify, and she let it, because this was a habit worth keeping.

At the door she stopped, quiz folded in her pocket, and took out her phone to photograph the sketch. "I still don't know if I'd have caught it on my own," she said. "Today, I mean. Without the red circle."

"That's not the question I'd ask," Mr. Crowchild said, and set the chewed pen back beside the register. "I'd ask whether you'll catch it Thursday."

"Quiz correction's due Thursday."

"Then there's your answer," he said, and rang up the next customer.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The GED tests were created in 1942 to let military service members and veterans who had not finished high school show high-school-level skills.
story:
Charlie had one hour before the ceremony and one mortarboard, which she was expected to wear, and one grandfather, who was currently sitting on the hood of his truck in the school parking lot refusing to come inside.

"Pop," she said, standing in front of him with her gown flapping open like a broken umbrella, "you cannot sit out here in the heat for two hours."

"I've sat in worse," he said. He was polishing his glasses with the end of his tie, which was a gesture that meant he was buying time. Behind them, families streamed toward the gym doors, mothers interposing themselves between toddlers and the parking lot's single landscaping boulder, which every child in town apparently needed to touch before graduation.

Kale arrived first, of course, because Kale arrived at everything like weather, sudden and cheerful. "Charlie, your grandfather is boycotting your graduation. I respect it. Is it a statement? Should I join?"

"It's not a statement," her grandfather said.

"It's a little bit of a statement," Charlie said.

Ms. Kobayashi crossed the lot with a stack of programs against her chest, saw the tableau, and changed course. "Mr. Alvarez. I have a folding chair with your name on it. Figuratively. It has duct tape on it, but so does everything in this school by June."

"You go on," he told her. "All of you. I'll watch from here. I've seen enough gyms."

Kale crouched by the truck bumper, negotiating, because Kale could not help himself. "What if we told you a secret about the ceremony? Insider information. There's a part where they read your name wrong."

"They'll read it right," Charlie said. "Alvarez is not hard."

"Charlie Alvarez," Kale attempted, mangling it into three syllables and a sneeze.

It was her grandfather, oddly, who laughed first, and then he did something Charlie had never seen him do: he reached into his wallet, which was older than her father, and pulled out a card soft with handling. She took it. It was a certificate of some kind, small, official, dated decades before she was born. At the top, in type she had to squint at, it said General Educational Development. His name below it. A GED.

"I never did this," he said, nodding at her gown, at the gym doors, at the whole apparatus of the morning. "I went in the Army instead, at seventeen, which your great-grandmother describes differently than I do. They made the GED tests in 1942, for service members and veterans who hadn't finished high school, so we could show we had the skills anyway. I took mine after I got out. I was the only one in my family with anything to put on a wall, and it wasn't even a wall certificate, it was a wallet one." He tapped it. "Genus: paperwork. Species: my whole education."

Charlie held the card very still. She had spent four years believing, in a vague and unexamined way, that the thing she was about to do in that gym was a door, and that people who didn't walk through it stayed outside. She had even said something like that to a boy in her civics class, junior year, about the deleterious effects of dropping out, and she'd felt righteous saying it. Now here was the counter-evidence, laminated and riding in the back pocket of a man who had raised her, who fixed her car, who read more than anyone she knew.

"So you're not coming in," she said, "because you never did."

"I'm not coming in because I'll cry in front of Kale."

"I would never document it," Kale said solemnly. "I would only tell everyone."

Mathieu pulled into the lot then, late, tie already around his forehead like a bandana, and leaned out the window. "Are we problem-solving or mourning? I can do either but not both in this heat."

Charlie looked at the card, then at the gym, then at her grandfather's shoes, which were polished, which meant he had intended, at some point this morning, to go in. The polished shoes were the tell. She tucked the certificate into her sleeve, behind the gown's inadequate pocket, where it made a small stiff line against her wrist.

"You're walking in with me," she said. "And when they read my name, I'm going to hold this up. Your certificate. Next to my diploma. Like a matched set."

"They'll think it's a protest."

"Let them," Charlie said, and she grabbed his sleeve the way he used to grab hers at the county fair, and Kale fell in behind them announcing to no one, "Genus: paperwork. Species: historic."

"Did I teach him that word today or was it already in him?" her grandfather asked.

"Honestly," Charlie said, pushing open the gym door, "with Kale you can never know."

Inside, the folding chairs with duct tape waited in rows, and somewhere near the front, one of them had his name on it, figuratively.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, adjourning, for when a group's work ends and members separate.
story:
The league had booked the park pavilion for the last Sunday in August, and by noon the tables were already sticky with soda and sheet cake. Nathaniel arrived carrying his cleats in one hand even though there was nothing left to play in them, because it seemed wrong to come without the equipment, as though he were a guest at his own funeral. The season had ended four days earlier with a loss in the semifinal, two to one, a game they had owned until the seventieth minute, and nobody had said much in the parking lot afterward. Now, under the pavilion's green roof, they were all pretending that the loss had amortized itself somehow, spread thin across enough hamburgers and stories that no single person had to carry it whole.

Bastien was at the grill in an apron that read KISS THE COOK, flipping burgers with a spatula he had clearly stolen from his own kitchen. He had been the one to suggest the party, back when the season was still alive and the idea of its ending had been abstract, a thing you could hold without weighing. "You're late," he said when he saw Nathaniel, though he was grinning. "You're late" was the team's whole vernacular, applied to everything from arriving at practice to losing a mark on a corner kick. Zackary sprawled across the bench beside him, ankle still taped from a sprain that had cost him the last three matches, holding a plate he had no intention of filling.

Ms. Choi, who had coached them for two seasons without ever raising her voice, moved among the tables with rolls of paper towels, and it struck Nathaniel that she was tidying things that did not need tidying, straightening a cooler, realigning a stack of cups, as if order could be imposed on the afternoon by hand. He set his cleats down on the bench and ate two burgers without tasting either. Around him the team was performing its usual rituals: the retelling of the semifinal with increasingly impossible saves, the mock scouting reports on each other's worst touches, the long gossip about who among the freshmen might actually be good next year.

Next year. The phrase kept snagging on something in him. Four of them were seniors, and this was the last time all fourteen would be in the same place at the same time, a fact everyone knew and no one was saying. He sat down at the end of the table with his phone, half to escape the noise, and typed something vague about groups ending, because he had a paper due in September on teamwork and had been putting off the reading. The search returned something he had never seen. In 1977, a researcher named Tuckman, working with Mary Ann Jensen, had added a fifth stage to a famous model of how groups develop, after the four stages everyone learned in school. The fifth stage was for when a group's work ends and the members separate.

He read it twice, then a third time, feeling something click into place that he could not yet name. "Zackary," he said, holding the phone out. "Look at this." Zackary leaned over, squinting against the sun. "What am I looking at." "There's a stage after everything else. It's called adjourning." Zackary read in silence, his thumb hovering over the screen, and when he looked up his expression had changed into something older. "So that's what this is," he said. "This party. We're in the literature."

Bastien abandoned the grill to see what they were reading, and then the three of them sat shoulder to shoulder over the small screen while burgers burned behind them and Ms. Choi rescued the last of them without comment. "It's kind of tautological when you think about it," Nathaniel said. "They made a stage for the fact that things end. Of course things end. You don't need a researcher to tell you the team breaks up in September." But even as he said it he could hear how the complaint rang hollow, because naming the thing did something. He had spent four days believing the semifinal loss was the wound, and now he understood the loss was only the surface of it, that the real thing underneath was this, the pavilion, the last hamburgers, the paper cups Ms. Choi kept straightening.

The seniors gathered near the water fountain for a photograph, and someone insisted the whole team be in it, all fourteen, plus Ms. Choi, who resisted and then didn't. The timer counted down and they stood in the slanting light with their arms around people they would gradually stop texting. Nathaniel thought about his two ideas of the day, the one that said naming an ending was redundant, and the one that said a name made the ending bearable, and found that he could hold both without either collapsing. He could not prove which was truer. He only knew that when Zackary had said we're in the literature, something in his chest had loosened slightly, like a knot worked free from the inside.

After the photo the party thinned the way parties do, by drift rather than decision. Ms. Choi shook each senior's hand and told each one something quiet and specific that Nathaniel couldn't hear. He ended up alone at the table with his cleats, laces coiled on the bench like something asleep. Behind him Bastien was arguing with Zackary about whether they could get one more pickup game going before everyone scattered to colleges in three different states, and Zackary was saying his ankle would hold for exactly one half, no more, and Bastien was already running toward the open grass with the ball at his feet. Nathaniel picked up the cleats and followed him onto the field, barefoot, the grass cold and wet between his toes.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: Under US federal law, workers aged 16 and 17 have no limit on working hours but may not be employed in jobs the Department of Labor has declared hazardous.
story:
The forty-two bus took the long way through the marsh roads in the afternoons, and Megan had learned to like that about it, because it gave her almost half an hour between the last bell and whatever came next. Today what came next was an interview at the garden center at five o'clock, and she spent the first mile staring at the practice questions she had copied into her notebook in blue ink. Tell me about yourself. Why do you want this job. Describe a time you handled a difficult customer. Beneath them, in smaller letters, she had written her mother's advice, which was look them in the eye and do not mumble, and beneath that, her own amendment, which was easier said than done.

Edwin dropped into the seat across the aisle, backpack first, and peered at the notebook. "You're rehearsing already? It's a garden center, not medical school."

"It's my first interview for anything," Megan said. "I would like to not sound like a neophyte, even if I am one."

"You won't. You're the least mumbly person I know." He said it without looking up from his phone, which somehow made it more convincing than if he had. She practiced the first answer anyway, low, aimed at the window rather than at him, and when she got through it without tripping she felt something in her chest loosen, not exactly confidence but its near neighbor.

Zayan boarded at the second stop, holding a paper bag from the deli on Route 9, and he sat down behind Edwin and leaned over the seat. "Guess who got offered a job," he said. "Same deli. Saturdays, and two evenings after closing, which is fine, and the owner wants me trained on the slicer by next month."

"Congratulations," Megan said, and then, because something snagged in her mind, "how old are you? Seventeen, right?"

"Until March." He tore the bag open and the smell of vinegar and cold cuts drifted forward. "Why?"

She didn't have a clean answer, only a memory of a handout from a career fair she'd attended mostly for the free pizza, a page she'd stuffed in a folder and half forgotten. Something about hours, something about hazardous. "There was a thing," she said slowly. "About what seventeen-year-olds can and can't do at work. I remember it being weird. Like, opposite of what you'd guess."

Zayan raised an eyebrow. "I can't work Saturdays?"

"No, it wasn't the hours." She took out her phone, typed labor laws 17 year olds, and scrolled while the bus swayed through the turns by the marsh, where the cattails stood in brown ranks and the water caught the late light in long streaks. Edwin leaned over to read too, his shadow falling across the screen.

The page from the Department of Labor was plainer than she expected. She read it twice, the second time aloud, quietly, so only the three of them could hear. "So workers who are sixteen and seventeen can work any number of hours. There's no limit at all. But they can't be employed in jobs the Department of Labor has declared hazardous."

"Hazardous," Edwin repeated. "Is a slicer hazardous?"

"There's a list," Megan said, scrolling further. She found it, a long catalog of machines and occupations, and ran her finger down the entries while Zayan chewed and watched. "Meat slicers are on it. That whole section's about power-driven meat-processing machines."

Zayan set down his sandwich half. "So I could work the counter all the hours in the world, but not the slicer. Not till I'm eighteen."

"That's what it says."

He was quiet for a moment, which for Zayan was a long time. "The owner's a decent guy, though. He probably doesn't know. His own kids are like thirty."

"Then tell him," Edwin said. "If he's decent, he'd rather know than get fined."

Megan looked at the page again, at the plain sentences that had rearranged her sense of how the world worked, that the danger was not in the hours but in the machines, that being almost an adult meant something specific and bureaucratic and real. She had assumed, before today, that the rules protected younger kids and then simply stopped, and it was strange and oddly invigorating to find that they had a shape, that seventeen sat in its own particular place with its own particular fence around it. She saved the page and texted Zayan the link.

"You know what's funny," Zayan said, balling up the deli bag, which still smelled like the job he might still take. "I was going to say yes to everything tomorrow. Whatever he asked. That was the whole plan. Say yes, be agreeable, get hired."

"That was my plan too," Megan admitted. "For the garden center. Say yes to whatever the shift is, smile, keep my eyes up." She glanced at her notebook, at her mother's handwriting visible through the page. "Maybe it's still mostly the plan. But not all of it."

"Interviews," Edwin said, as the bus slowed at her stop, "are just conversations where everyone's pretending to be taller."

She slid her notebook into her bag and stood, gripping the cold metal pole, and looked back at the two of them, Zayan with his phone already open to the link, Edwin with his feet up on the seat. "Wish me eye contact," she said.

"Eye contact," they said together, and she stepped down into the blue evening, already practicing her first sentence under her breath as she crossed the parking lot toward the lit door of the garden center.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: In 2023, the US unemployment rate was 3.9 percent for workers aged 25 and over with a high school diploma and 5.6 percent for those without one.
story:
Zoey stood at the kitchen doorway holding her cap in both hands, watching her grandmother unfold napkins into crowns for the place settings. The dining table had been extended with the leaf that only came out twice a year, and down the center ran a procession of dishes: her mother's lemon rice, an aunt's fried fish, a bowl of something with rosemary that nobody had claimed yet. Her diploma lay propped against the fruit bowl like a hostage.

Anissa arrived first, still in her work uniform from the pharmacy, smelling faintly of hand sanitizer and vanilla. She dropped into the chair beside Zoey and pulled out her phone. "You have to see Aaryan's post," she said. "He put up that he's job hunting again."

Zoey scrolled through the photo. Aaryan, who had left school halfway through junior year to help at his uncle's shop, stood outside a warehouse with his thumbs up, and under it he had written two words: fifth interview. The shop had closed in the spring. She thought about messaging him and then set the phone face down on the tablecloth, because the relatives were arriving, and relatives arriving meant questions with the precision of dental work.

Her uncle asked about her major, undetermined. Her mother's cousin asked about her major, undecided. Mr. Nair, the retired teacher from three doors down who had been invited because he had once lent Zoey's father a ladder and never quite returned to being a stranger, asked nothing at all, which Zoey found so invigorating that she nearly hugged him. He ate the rosemary dish, whatever it was, and complimented the cook, who turned out to be her father, who turned out to be modest about it for exactly one round of praise.

Between the main course and dessert, Anissa leaned over and said, "He told me the numbers, you know. He's been keeping track, like a spreadsheet, because nobody believes him."

"Numbers about what?"

"About how it actually is out there. He found this thing from 2023. For people twenty-five and older with just a high school diploma, unemployment was 3.9 percent. Without one, 5.6." She wiped her fingers on the paper crown napkin. "He says every time someone tells him school doesn't matter, he wants to show them the spreadsheet. But he also says it's not that simple, because his uncle had a diploma and the shop still closed."

Zoey turned her water glass a quarter turn on the tablecloth. The putative lesson of the evening, delivered in toasts and in her grandmother's grip on her wrist, was that the diploma meant everything, that it was a door, a key, a shield. But Anissa's numbers had a different texture. They were small, 3.9 against 5.6, a difference you could hold in one hand, and yet behind each decimal point stood whole lives doing interviews and spreadsheets and warehouse parking lots. She wondered whether the numbers described a door or merely a slight easing of the wind. She wondered whether Aaryan regretted leaving, or whether regret was the wrong shape for it entirely.

Dessert was her favorite, semolina with cashews, and her mother stood to give a speech about how Zoey would begin college in the fall and how the family had sacrificed and how Zoey's grandfather, the putative patriarch of every gathering though he had died before she was born, would have been proud. Zoey smiled in the right places. Under the table she texted Aaryan: congratulations on the fifth interview. Do you want me to send you the career center listings from my school? They let alumni use them, and maybe friends of alumni, she wasn't sure, she could find out.

His reply came while the dishes were being stacked. Maybe, he wrote. Come by the shop Saturday. Not the uncle's old one. The new one. I'm doing inventory.

She looked up from the phone at the table, at the crumpled napkin crowns and the diploma still leaning against the fruit bowl, and she thought about sabbaticals, which Mr. Nair had mentioned over dessert, a year away from teaching that had turned into three, and how everyone at the table had taken some version of a detour and landed somewhere they hadn't planned. She did not know yet whether she would go on Saturday, or whether the listings would help, or whether the difference between 3.9 and 5.6 was the kind of thing that bent a life or just described one already bent.

"I'll bring coffee," she texted back.

He sent a thumbs up, the same one from the warehouse photo, and across the table her grandmother caught her eye and raised the teapot in a small, wordless toast.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that everyone aged 13 to 64 be tested for HIV at least once as part of routine health care.
story:
Tyson had agreed to it in a moment of confidence he no longer possessed. Ms. Novák had asked for volunteers to co-teach the freshman health unit on consent and contraception, and Adriel had elbowed him until his hand went up, and now it was Saturday and the presentation was Monday and he knew almost nothing he could say out loud.

He was at his grandmother's house because she was convalescing after a knee replacement, and his mother thought he should keep her company, and he thought the drive would give him time to rehearse. He sat at the kitchen table with a legal pad and his phone propped against the sugar bowl, FaceTiming Adriel.

"Okay," Adriel said. "Start from the top. Consent."

"It has to be freely given," Tyson said. "And specific, and reversible. You can say yes to one thing and no to another, and you can change your mind halfway through." He had read that in four places the night before, and it had stopped sounding like a slogan and started sounding like a description of how anything decent worked, like returning a borrowed thing or leaving a party.

"Say it like it's not a legal pad talking." Adriel held up his own notes, which were a drawing of a dog. "Freshmen can smell a legal pad."

Tyson tried again, plainer, using an example about asking before taking someone's fries, and Adriel nodded, so he kept going. Contraception was harder. He laid out what he knew: condoms, hormonal methods, the clinic downtown that saw people under eighteen without calling parents first. Then he stopped.

"Here's the part I actually know something about," he said. "At my physical in August, the doctor offered me an HIV test. I thought she suspected something. I panicked a little, honestly. But she said no, it's routine. The CDC recommends everyone aged thirteen to sixty-four get tested for HIV at least once as part of routine health care. Thirteen. Like, you walk in for a sports physical and they just offer it."

"That's not that old," Adriel said.

"It's my age. It's freshman age." Tyson wrote the numbers on the pad because they seemed like the kind of thing that would slide off him otherwise. He had sat in the paper-gowned silence of that exam room feeling accused, and then the accusation had dissolved and left something else, the fact that a whole country had decided this was ordinary. Not a punishment. Not a judgment. Just maintenance, the same as blood pressure.

He tried to say that to Adriel and it came out as two philosophies colliding, one being the way his grandfather had talked about the body, as a private matter between a man and his conscience, and the other being what the doctor's office assumed, that bodies were things that got checked. His grandfather would have called the second one cold rationalism, Tyson supposed, machines and checklists where there should be shame or dignity or silence. But the checklist had caught a friend of his mother's early, that was the story she'd told him in the car afterward, unprompted, and the woman was fine now.

His grandmother came in on her walker and made him move the sugar bowl so she could sit. She asked what he was doing and he told her, half expecting her to leave the room. She said her mother had buried two sisters in 1934 and nobody had been able to say what from, not to children, not to anyone, and that if somebody had offered those women a test, they would have taken the bus to it. Then she told him to make her tea and stopped contributing, which he understood to be her version of support.

He went back to the phone. Tate had joined the call from a bus, headphones on, arguing the other side: that the doctor's offer had probably still been coded, that they asked you questions in a certain order and watched your face, and that routine for the system wasn't the same as routine for the kid in the paper gown. Tyson wrote that down too. It seemed to him that both things could be true at once, that the test could be ordinary and the moment of offering it could be delicate, and that his job Monday was to say the first thing without erasing the second. What he still didn't know was how to say any of it without sounding like he had all the answers, because he had a legal pad and one doctor's appointment and that was it.

At the counter he poured the tea and Tate was still talking and Adriel was still drawing the dog. Tyson tore the numbers off the top of the pad and folded them into his shirt pocket. "Okay," he said. "One more time from the top."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut's dual process model describes grieving people as moving back and forth between facing the loss and getting on with rebuilding daily life, rather than moving in one direction.
story:
The vending machine on the fourth floor ate Morgan's dollar twice before surrendering a bag of pretzels she didn't want. She wanted to be doing something with her hands, and buying was doing something. Down the corridor, past the doors marked with numbers and small crosses of tape, her grandmother lay in room 412 with the machines already quiet, and the family stood in the hallway discussing parking validations as though parking were the subject of the evening. Morgan's mother was explaining, for the third time, why she hadn't moved her car. Her aunt was being patient in the way that meant she wasn't.

"You could go in," her aunt said to Morgan, gently, and Morgan said she would in a minute, and then spent the minute refolding the pretzel bag into smaller and smaller squares. It felt obscene, somehow, that the hallway smelled like lemon floor cleaner and someone's microwaved soup, that the world kept producing smells. She went in. The room was warm in the wrong way, an overheated stillness, and her grandmother's hands looked like they were still deciding what to do. Morgan held one, said something she couldn't remember afterward, and left before she could decide whether crying was required or forbidden.

The funeral was on a Tuesday. On Friday, Foster texted Morgan asking if she wanted to see the new monster movie, the one with the enormous screaming crab, and Morgan said yes before she had finished thinking about it. She laughed so hard at one point that popcorn went down the wrong pipe, and then in the parking lot afterward she sat in Foster's car with the door open and her feet on the asphalt, feeling like a criminal. "That was actually good," Foster said, oblivious. "The crab had layers." Morgan said she had a great time, and the words tasted like a confession.

She confessed it, finally, to her aunt on Sunday, while the two of them were sorting her grandmother's cookbook shelf, deciding which spines were coming home and which were going to the church sale. There was a pencil mark beside a recipe for lemon squares, dated 1987, and Morgan held the page open while she talked, because it was easier to accuse herself at somebody else's book. "I laughed at a movie," she said. "Five days after. Like it never happened. What is wrong with me." She expected her aunt to denigrate her honesty, or worse, to comfort her, and she braced for both.

Her aunt didn't do either. She pulled a folded photocopied page out of her coat pocket, soft at the creases from handling, and smoothed it on the counter between the flour and the salt. It was from a hospice pamphlet, she said, someone had given it to her at the front desk the night it happened, and she had read it in the parking garage four times. "It's called the dual process model," she said. Morgan read it herself, slowly, the way she read things she suspected of being a trick. Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut, the page said, described grieving people as moving back and forth between facing the loss and getting on with rebuilding daily life, rather than moving in one direction. Back and forth. Not a river you fell into and were carried away by. A tide, or a person pacing a room.

"So the movie," Morgan said, "counts as rebuilding." Her aunt said that was her reading of it, and that page nine had annoyed her, and that she'd argued with it out loud in the garage, which had made a man collecting his ticket jump. Morgan laughed, which felt strange and then, gradually, didn't. "You yelled at a pamphlet," she said. "I denigrate your methodology but admire your energy." Her aunt threw a dish towel at her.

That didn't mean the pacing was gentle. On Wednesday Morgan skipped lunch to sit in the library with her headphones on, sullen and unreachable, and let Leane believe she was studying for chemistry. She wasn't studying. She was looking at a photograph of her grandmother holding a sycophantic orange cat who had adored her only when the food bowl was full, and Morgan had said so at the time, and her grandmother had said, "Of course, that's why we understand each other." Morgan smiled at the memory and then, without warning, was crying at a library table, quietly, the way you learn to do in public, and Leane appeared with two milks from the cafeteria and set one down without a word and didn't leave.

Morgan wasn't sure, later, how much of it she believed. She knew the tide went out and the tide came back, and she trusted that now the way she trusted the tide having a schedule, not in the sense of being spared. She knew she would keep laughing and keep sitting in warm rooms holding still hands in her memory, and that she could not say which one was the true her and suspected the question was badly formed. At the church sale the following Saturday she bought back her grandmother's cookbook for a dollar, out of the donation box, from a volunteer who didn't know it had ever belonged to anyone, and the woman said, "You look like you got a deal," and Morgan said, "I did," and slid the lemon squares page to the front so she could find it again.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: The 1996 book Continuing Bonds, by Dennis Klass, Phyllis Silverman and Steven Nickman, argued that keeping a lasting connection with someone who has died is a normal part of grief, not a failure to move on.
story:
The temple smelled of incense and oranges, and Jade sat in the third row with a recipe card in her coat pocket, running her thumb along its bent corner while the monk chanted. Her grandmother had died nine days ago, in a hospital bed with the blinds half open, and today everyone kept telling Jade to let her rest, to release her, to move forward. Jade had not told anyone that she still said good evening to the photograph on the kitchen shelf, or that on Tuesday she had asked it whether the congee needed more ginger, and then added more ginger, and it had been right.

Jules slid into the pew beside her and pressed a tissue into her hand without comment. Behind them, Simon argued quietly with his own tie, which he had borrowed from an uncle and could not knot. Before the service Mr. Yip, who had run the temple's kitchen for thirty years and had known her grandmother longer than that, had stopped Jade in the doorway, looked at her a long moment, and said only, "She talked about you every week. Every single week." He had not said anything else, which somehow made it heavier.

After the chanting there was food, and people stood in clots in the courtyard saying things that were meant kindly and landed strangely. An aunt told Jade that grief was like a muscle; if you didn't use it, it would atrophy, and if you used it too much it would tear, and Jade had no idea what to do with that. Jules rescued her with a question about the recipe card, which Jade had taken out to show her.

"She wrote the measurements like this," Jade said. 'A handful. More than you think. Stop before it looks right.' That's not a recipe, that's a conversation. I cook from them and I talk to her while I do it, and I don't know if that's healthy or if I'm just refusing to accept it." Jules said it sounded healthy to her. Simon, arriving with his tie finally knotted and immediately crooked again, said his therapist had a word for something like that but he couldn't remember it, and then apologized for being tangential, which he claimed was his whole personality.

What Jade could not say out loud was the worry underneath: that everyone here believed the dead should be released, and that she was failing a test she hadn't known she was taking. Her mother wanted the recipe cards boxed for storage. "You can't build a life around them," she had said last night, gently, which was the gentlest form of a hard thing.

When the courtyard emptied, Mr. Yip caught her at the kitchen door. "She left a box," he said. "Told me months ago you should have it. Not your mother. You." He brought it out from behind the rice cooker, a shoebox bound with rubber bands gone brittle. Inside were photographs, a folded scarf, and beneath everything a paperback so worn its spine had gone pale: Continuing Bonds, by Dennis Klass, Phyllis Silverman and Steven Nickman, 1996 printed under the title. Jade had never heard of it. The front cover promised new understandings of grief.

But the twist was not the book. The twist was the recipe cards tucked inside it, in her grandmother's handwriting but older, softer, faded blue: the same cards Jade had at home were copies. These originals were covered in marginal notes. "Mama, too much salt again," one said, dated years before Jade was born. Another: "Mama, Jules's grandmother made yours at New Year and cried, so I made it too." Her grandmother had cooked from her own dead mother's cards and talked to her while she cooked, for decades, and had found a book that said this was not a failure to move on, and had kept both hidden in a kitchen where nobody thought to look.

Jade sat down on a stack of rice sacks. Jules read over her shoulder. Simon leaned in the doorway, uncharacteristically silent. "So it has a name," Jade said at last, tapping the cover. "Continuing Bonds." She laughed once, a wet, startled sound. "She found the word for it thirty years before I needed it and never told me. She just left it behind the rice."

Her mother appeared in the doorway then, and Jade held up one of the old cards, the salt one, and watched her mother's face change. "You're taking these home," her mother said, which was not what she had said last night, and Jade understood that her mother was also holding a card somewhere, somewhere Jade had never seen, and that neither of them would say so.

At home that evening, Jade boiled water and measured out rice with her hands. "Okay," she said to the kitchen shelf, to the photograph, to whatever was listening or nothing. "More than you think." She reached for the ginger.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: Encapsulation means hiding a class's data behind methods, so other code can use the object without depending on how it stores its data.
story:
The practice field was three folding tables pushed together under gym lights, and the robot, Nicole's robot, was sitting dead on its side with its arm bent at a angle arms should not bend. She had been in the corner rewriting the arm controller for two hours, and Slade kept coming over to say it was fine, it was fine, we'll just re-zero the encoder before the next match, and each time she said okay and did not look up from her laptop.

The problem was not the encoder. The problem was that the arm code had started its life as something Brittany wrote back in October, and Brittany had done what they all did then: a public variable for the angle, another for the speed, and a comment that said do not touch this in a way that made everyone touch it. Six months of quick fixes had grown on top of it like mold on bread. Nicole's fix from last night, the one that was supposed to make the arm stop drifting, had instead made the robot score in the wrong goal once, in practice, in front of Mr. Sutton and a recruiter from the state school who kept saying the word monetize as if their little club was a startup.

"There's teams that just rebuild," Brittany said, dropping onto the floor beside her with a granola bar. "Day before regionals, I mean. Nobody does."

"I'm not rebuilding the robot. I'm rebuilding the code."

"That's worse."

Nicole turned the laptop so Brittany could see. "Everything reads arm.speed. Everything. The drive code, the autonomous, Slade's little status display. If I change how speed works, all of it breaks."

"So don't change it."

"So it drifts forever."

Brittany chewed, watching the practice field where a team in matching jackets was running a clean autonomous loop. "Mr. Sutton said something about that once. Hiding things."

"Mr. Sutton says a lot of things."

"He said encapsulation means hiding a class's data behind methods. I wrote it on my hand and it washed off."

Nicole had a vague memory of that lesson, October, half-attended, the day she'd been fighting with the fundraising forms. She opened the slide deck anyway and there it was, a rectangle with little padlocks, and the line Brittany remembered, and a phrase underneath she had never actually read: other code can use the object without depending on how it stores its data. She read it three times. It was such a boring sentence. It was also, she realized with the specific nausea of a deadline, the answer, and it had been sitting in a folder since October while she built six months of dependencies on Brittany's variables.

"You're smiling," Brittany said. "That's creepy."

"I'm making the fields private. All of them. Then getters."

"Nicole. Qualification matches start in an hour."

"It's not that much. Watch." She was already typing. The arm became a class, ArmController, with its angle and its speed locked away where nothing could reach in and set them behind its back, and one method to ask for the current angle and one to ask for the speed. Getters. Then she could fix the drift inside the class, quietly, without any of the other code knowing anything had changed, because none of it had ever needed to know how the numbers were stored. It only needed to ask.

Slade materialized behind them with two waters and zero patience. "Encoder. Re-zero. We talked about this."

"It's not the encoder. Look, run the status display."

He leaned in, arms crossed, radiating the impermeable confidence of a person who has been told the plan and intends for the plan to hold. The display came up. Arm angle: 47.2. He tapped the screen. "See, fine."

"That's not the old code reading the variable. That's my getter. I changed how the arm works underneath and your display didn't break."

"Because it's fine."

"Because it can't see the fields anymore. Try to set arm.speed directly. Go on."

He took the keyboard, typed, and the compiler refused him in red. He stared at it. "You did this on purpose."

"An hour ago I did it in a panic."

It took forty minutes to convert the rest, Slade grumbling, Brittany quietly handing over the autonomous file before he asked twice. Once, mid-conversion, the drive code threw an error and Nicole felt the whole veneer of competence she'd been wearing all season crack straight down the middle, but the error was a typo, one bracket, and she fixed it with hands she kept steady by force.

The arm ran clean. Not perfect. In the first qualification match it still overshot the mid goal by a finger's width, and they lost by six points, and Slade said nothing the whole walk back to the pit. She sat down and opened the laptop again, because inside the class now there was one place to look instead of forty, and one number to turn, and she knew which one. Whether the number was right she would not know until the next match, and she said so, out loud, to nobody in particular.

"That's it?" Slade said, standing over her. "You don't know?"

"I don't know. Ask me after."

"Whatever you did," Brittany said, "the display still works."

Nicole turned the dial, two degrees, and deployed.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: In Kazuo Ishiguro's 1989 novel The Remains of the Day, the butler Stevens reports events accurately but misreads their meaning, including his own feelings.
story:
The bell over the door had a crack in it, so it rang flat, and Felix heard it ring behind him three times that afternoon before he understood he was going in circles. The essay was due Monday. Ms. Leung had assigned The Remains of the Day and asked one question: can we trust the narrator? Felix had written half a page, deleted it, written it again, and now he was standing in the travel section of the secondhand bookshop on Miller Street, holding a paperback with a cracked spine and pretending to read about walking in Devon.

"You've read that page four times," said Heidi, appearing beside him with an armful of remainders. She worked Saturdays, shelving, mostly to be near books she couldn't afford. "Also that's the travel section. Devon is not a novel."

"I know where I am," Felix said, which was untrue in several ways. The trouble was that Stevens, the butler, kept saying sensible things in a reasonable voice, and Felix kept believing him, and then something would happen on the page that didn't fit, like a drawer that wouldn't close, and he couldn't say why. He had a paragraph in his notebook that read: Stevens says he felt X. Stevens did Y. So? He had written "So?" six times and underlined it twice.

Seth arrived at four, smelling of the pool, his hair still wet at the collar. He dropped into the reading chair by the window and picked up Felix's notes without asking. "This is the butler book. The guy drives around England thinking about his life. That's it? That's the whole plot?"

"He does more than think about his life," Felix said. "He thinks about it wrongly." As soon as he said it, he felt the drawer slide shut. "He's not lying, though. That's the thing. He reports everything accurately. The dates, the conversations, what people said. He gets the facts right and then he misreads what the facts mean. Including his own feelings. He'll say he felt pride in his work, and meanwhile he's describing a scene where he's obviously heartbroken, and he just, doesn't clock it."

Seth looked at him over the notebook. "Bro, you just wrote your thesis statement out loud."

Ms. Leung came over from the register, which she was closing early because the till was short again, the shop flirting with insolvency the way it had for thirty years, daring the landlord to notice. She set down two cups of tea nobody had ordered. "What did he say out loud?"

"Something about a butler," Heidi said.

"Stevens," Felix said, and found, warming his hands on the cup, that he could say it more carefully now. "He says he felt one thing and does another. The point of view is first person, everything filtered through him, so the reader has to trust him for the facts and distrust him for the meaning at the same time. It's like believing a weather report and doubting the weatherman's commentary on it."

Ms. Leung smiled into her tea. "That's a better sentence than most of my students managed when I taught."

"You taught?"

"English. Before the blase years, when I decided I preferred books to classrooms." She tapped his notebook. "Your problem isn't the argument. Your problem is that you want certainty from a book that's specifically about a man who cannot be certain about himself. Write the uncertainty in. It's not a flaw in your essay. It's the essay."

Felix sat with that. He turned to Heidi, who was reshelving a guidebook on coastal walks with unnecessary force. "Does that sound right? That I can hold both things? Like, Stevens is reliable about events and unreliable about what the events mean, and I have to say both without picking one?"

"That's how I feel about my dad's letters from before the divorce," Heidi said, not turning around. "Everything in them happened. Every single detail is true. And the meaning he gives it is a different story entirely." She pushed the guidebook flush against its neighbours. "So yes. It sounds right. It sounds like people."

Seth had gone blase about the whole conversation somewhere around the second thesis statement and was reading the back of a spy thriller, but he looked up long enough to say, "Write the essay, don't desiccate it into five bullet points like you did for the last one. Mr. Okafor said your Hamlet paper read like a receipt."

That evening Felix sat in the window bay after closing, which Ms. Leung permitted when the weather was bad, and wrote. He wrote the sentence about facts and meanings. He wrote a paragraph about a scene where Stevens's father dies during a dinner service and Stevens continues serving, calling it his moment of triumph, and Felix let the contradiction sit there without smoothing it over, because the reader would see it the way he had seen it, slowly, like a shape in fog. At the bottom of the page he wrote a question he couldn't answer yet: is Stevens honest, then, or just accurate? He underlined it once, left it, and started packing his bag.

Ms. Leung locked the till and handed him the paperback with the cracked spine. "Bring it back whenever," she said. "It's been on that shelf long enough to know the way home."

He walked out into the rain with the book dry under his jacket, already composing the opening line in his head.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: SQL was developed at IBM in the early 1970s by Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce, and was first called SEQUEL.
story:
Charlotte's laptop sat open on the kitchen table between a bowl of unfinished cereal and her mother's account ledger, and on the screen were two tables: customers and orders, twenty names in one, forty rows in the other. The assignment from Ms. Chan was a single sentence. Write a query that finds which customers never ordered anything.

She had started at nine. It was now eleven and she had a working answer she did not trust, because it used a subquery with NOT IN, and Ms. Chan had circled something like that on the board last week and written "there is a better way" beside it in green pen.

Her phone buzzed against the table. Kaden, from the class group chat, had sent a voice note. "Charlotte. Settle this. Antonia says you pronounce it S-Q-L, each letter, and I've been saying sequel my whole life. She's saying I sound like an idiot."

Charlotte called him. She could hear Antonia in the background, close enough to be sitting on the same bed, which meant they were studying together without her again.

"It's spelled S-Q-L," Antonia said, loud enough to come through the phone's small speaker. "So you spell it out."

"That's not how acronyms work. You don't say U-S-A."

"You do sometimes."

Charlotte put the phone on the table, propped against the milk carton, and opened a new browser tab while they argued. She typed the history of the language into the search bar, half to end the argument and half because she was congenitally incapable of leaving a dispute unresolved, a trait her mother called charming and her teachers called exhausting.

The first result settled it. "Kaden's right," she said. "SQL was developed at IBM in the early 1970s by Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce. And it was first called SEQUEL. That's where his pronunciation comes from."

There was a silence on the other end, then Kaden's voice, gratified and insufferable. "Say it again, Antonia. Slower."

Antonia said something Charlotte couldn't hear, and then, closer to the phone: "Fine. It was first called SEQUEL. But I'm still spelling it out, because that's what everyone at my internship does."

Charlotte said that seemed fair, that both could be right, and Kaden said that was the most Canadian thing she had ever said. She hung up because the better way had started forming in her head, the way answers sometimes did, arriving all at once and slightly out of order.

If the problem was finding what was missing, then she did not want to search for absence directly. She wanted to keep everything and then look at what came back empty. She typed LEFT JOIN customers and wrote the join so that every customer appeared whether or not they had orders, and then added WHERE the order's id IS NULL, which would leave only the rows where the join had found nothing to attach. She ran it. Three names came back: H. Rasmussen, P. Okonkwo, M. Delacroix. Customers who had signed up and never bought a thing.

She sat back. It was a small, clean machine, and she liked it more than she had expected to like anything in this course. Her mother came through the kitchen doorway with a laundry basket on her hip and stopped to look at the screen.

"Is that my ledger?"

Charlotte hesitated, then decided not to prevaricate. She had imported her mother's spreadsheet that morning, thinking real data would be better practice than Ms. Chan's sample tables, and she had not mentioned it. "I put the shop's customers into a database. It was either that or fake names. Yours were better."

Her mother set the basket down and pulled a chair around beside her. "So who's my dead weight?"

"Nobody's dead weight. Three people registered and never ordered. One of them is M. Delacroix." She watched her mother's face change as she read the name. "Who's that?"

"Marcel. He signed the guest book at the winter open house. I spoke to him for forty minutes about the ceramics." Her mother was quiet for a moment, then laughed, a short sound, not quite happy. "There's an epigram for you. The ones who talk the longest buy the least."

Charlotte saved the file under a new name before she could be told not to, because the data was hers now too, three ghosts in a table that Ms. Chan would never see. On Monday she would hand in the query against the sample data, and the join would do its work, and no one would know that somewhere in her laptop the same four lines of code had found a man who liked her mother's pottery enough to leave his name and not enough to buy it.

"Can it tell you the other way around?" her mother asked. "Orders with no customer?"

Charlotte looked at the query, then copied it, and began swapping the table names.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: A 1950 study by Leon Festinger, Stanley Schachter and Kurt Back in student housing found that people living closer together, or near shared stairways, were more likely to become friends.
story:
The party was Skylar's idea, held in Ms. Tehrani's backyard because Ms. Tehrani had the only fence tall enough that the neighbors didn't call about noise. Sienna arrived with her duffel bag already in the car, because the movers came at six in the morning and she was leaving straight from the party, sleeping in the new house's empty rooms. Somebody had strung lights between the plum trees. Leighton was manning the grill with the seriousness of a surgeon, and Skylar kept refilling Sienna's cup with lemonade she didn't want, as if hydration could slow the clock.

"You could still not go," Skylar said, halfway through the second hour. "People defer a semester all the time."

"Defer and do what, live in your basement?"

"Live in my basement," Skylar said, and they both laughed, and the laugh was the friable kind, crumbling at the edges the moment it finished.

The trouble started later, near the bonfire, when Sienna tried to explain why she wasn't as wrecked as everyone seemed to need her to be. Ms. Tehrani had lent her a book in June, after the last day of classes, something about how friendships actually form, and one study had stuck with her. "It's from 1950," she said, poking at the fire with a stick she'd found. "Leon Festinger, Stanley Schachter, Kurt Back. They looked at student housing." Leighton turned the sausages without looking up. "And the people who lived closer together, or near the shared stairways, were more likely to become friends. That was it. Not similar interests, not compatible personalities. Distance."

"So what," Skylar said, "you're saying friendship is an accident of where the stairs are."

"I'm saying it's partly that. Partly." Sienna watched a coal split and fall. "I found it in that book Ms. Tehrani gave me, and at first it made me furious, like everything we built was just, I don't know, epidemiology. Like proximity spreads through a dorm and we caught each other."

Leighton flipped a sausage too hard and it rolled into the grass. "That's a cheerful thing to tell your friends at your own farewell party."

But Sienna was building toward something, and she could feel Skylar bracing against it, so she pushed through. She told them about her orientation packet, about how she'd already looked at the floor plan of her residence, how she'd emailed housing and asked, with an embarrassment she could still feel in her face, to be placed near the stairwell. "I parametrized it," she said. "That sounds insane. I made a little spreadsheet. Room numbers, distance to the stairs, distance to the laundry, because the study said the stairways were what mattered, and I requested one of those rooms. And I got it. Room 3C, right by the stairs."

The silence after that lasted long enough for the fire to pop twice. Skylar set her cup down on the fence post with exaggerated care. "So we're the stairwell," she said. "That's what you're telling me. We lived near the stairs of each other and now you've found new stairs."

"No. That's the part I keep getting wrong and then getting right again." Sienna put her stick down. "The study says where you start. It doesn't say anything about nine years of Skylar knowing my locker combination, or Leighton driving me to my grandmother's funeral. Those aren't stairways. But I can't pretend the stairs are nothing either, because when I get there in August, the first person I talk to will probably be the girl across the hall, and she'll probably matter to me in a year, and none of that will have anything to do with who either of us is."

"That's the most depressing comfort I've ever heard," Leighton said, but he was smiling a little, and he handed her the first sausage off the grill, the ceremonial one, the one he always burned on purpose because she'd once claimed burned ones tasted better and he'd never let her take it back.

Ms. Tehrani came out with a tray of cups and said nothing about any of it, only that the noise ordinance technically applied after eleven. Skylar linked her arm through Sienna's and walked her to the gate, past the plum trees, and stood there while Sienna looked back once at the lit yard, the fire, Leighton rescuing another sausage from the coals. "Room 3C," Skylar said. "Near the stairs. Text me the first thing the girl across the hall says to you."

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: On 28 March 1979, the UK government of James Callaghan lost a vote of no confidence by a single vote, 311 to 310, forcing a general election.
story:
Aaron had three days to learn the difference between how a parliament chooses a head of government and how a presidential republic does, and he had chosen to do it at his grandfather's house, where the wifi was bad and the silence was worse. His notes sat open on the kitchen table between a bowl of walnuts and a crossword his grandfather had abandoned at the halfway point. He had written "PM chosen by the party in the legislature" and then, underneath, "President chosen separately by voters," and then he had stopped, because the two lines looked equally thin to him, as though neither of them could hold the weight of an actual country.

"What are you frowning at?" his grandfather asked, carrying two mugs of tea he had not been asked for.

"A test. On Friday." Aaron turned the notebook so the old man could see. "Comparing systems. How they pick a leader and how they get rid of one."

His grandfather set the mugs down slowly, and Aaron noticed that he did not look at the page so much as at the table itself, the way people look at a spot when they are deciding whether to speak. "Mm," he said at last. "Get rid of one. Yes." He tapped the crossword twice with one finger and left the room.

That was the first strange thing, though Aaron did not know it yet. The second was the box.

He found it that afternoon while looking for the spare blanket his grandfather kept saying was in the hall cupboard. The box was behind the vacuum, a biscuit tin gone dull with age, and inside it were newspaper clippings, yellowed and soft at the edges. He read the date at the top of the front page before anything else, March 1979, and then the headline, and then he stopped breathing for a second. On 28 March 1979, the government of James Callaghan had lost a vote of no confidence by a single vote, 311 to 310, forcing a general election. One vote. He read it three times. The paper in his hands said it plainly, the way papers say things that happened, and Aaron, who had been arguing only the night before on the phone with Willem that a single vote was a rounding error in the life of a nation, sat down on the hallway floor with the tin in his lap.

Willem had said what Aaron's whole class tended to say, that elections were decided by millions and that individual votes were decorative, a ritual people performed to feel like citizens rather than subjects. Frederic had taken the opposite line, that not voting was how you quietly handed the country to whoever was most obdurate about showing up, a slow slide toward oligarchy by abstention. Aaron had equivocated between them on the phone, saying both were kind of right, and had hated himself a little for it, because both could not be kind of right, not about this.

He carried the tin into the kitchen and set it on the table beside his notes. "Grandad. What is this?"

His grandfather was at the sink with his back turned. He did not move for long enough that Aaron heard the tap drip twice.

"Where did you find that."

"The cupboard. It's a vote of no confidence. It's in my book too, but the book just says it happened." Aaron paused, because the old man's shoulders had gone very still, and stillness in his grandfather usually preceded either a joke or a door closing. "You kept it in a tin. Like it was something."

His grandfather dried his hands, taking his time with each finger, and then came and sat down and turned the clipping so it faced him, the right way up, as though it could only be read by him. "It was something," he said. "I was there."

"There where."

"In the lobby. That night." He laid one finger on the page, not on the headline but below it, on the list of names printed small, the division list, names in two columns, and Aaron looked where the finger pointed and did not understand until he saw the name beside the finger and saw that it was the same name as the man sitting across from him, younger by forty-six years, printed in a newspaper.

"You voted," Aaron said.

"I was a member. One term, that was all, backbench, you'd never have heard of me." His grandfather turned the mug in his hands without drinking. "It came down to the last few names being read out. You could hear the tellers counting. Eleven to ten, they said, three hundred and eleven to three hundred and ten, and the government fell, and I stood there knowing my legs had carried me into one lobby and not the other."

Aaron looked at his notebook, at his two thin lines about how parliaments and presidents choose and remove leaders, and they looked different now, thicker, load-bearing. In a presidential system the man in the tin could not have done that; a president sits fixed for a term, and there is no lobby, no single night when the floor tilts on one pair of feet. He wrote that down, then crossed out "the floor tilts" because it sounded like something from a poem, then wrote it again underneath, smaller, where maybe Ms. Gill wouldn't read it.

"So when Willem says one vote doesn't matter," Aaron said slowly, "he's wrong. It's not even an opinion. It's a fact with a date."

"Once," his grandfather said. "It mattered once, on that night, in that place. Most nights it doesn't. I won't tell you which kind of night Friday's test is, because I don't know, and neither do you." He closed the tin's lid with a small click. "But I'll tell you one thing I never put in any speech. I still don't know if I was right."

Aaron stared at him. "You were on the winning side."

"The winning side," his grandfather said, "and I have wondered about it for forty-six years." He pushed the tin across the table toward Aaron. "Take it to your test if you like. Mind you bring it back."

Aaron put the tin in his bag, between the notebook and the calculator, and felt the weight of it settle against his books.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: Google added 'search by image' in 2011, letting users upload a picture or paste its link to find where else it appears on the web.
story:
The video arrived at 7:14 in the morning, while Ashton was eating cereal at the kitchen counter: a grainy clip of a flooded street, a man clinging to a stop sign, water the color of milk tea rushing past the mailboxes. His grandmother had sent it to eleven people. "Share this before they take it down," she had written, "this is the storm heading toward us Thursday."

Ashton put his spoon down. There was no storm heading toward them Thursday. He was eighteen and had spent the previous evening arguing with his mother about whether he could skip his Saturday shift at her office to visit Elliana at her college an hour away, and his grandmother's forwarded clip felt like one more thing being handed to him, already decided, already urgent. But he had learned something in Mr. Suzuki's class the year before, something half-remembered, about pictures that traveled farther than the truth attached to them.

He typed into his phone: can a video lie about where it happened. The results were noisy. Then he found it, the thing he was looking for, buried in an article about checking sources: Google had added search by image in 2011, so anyone could upload a picture or paste its link and find where else it appeared on the web. He read the sentence twice. It was that simple and that old, older than his little cousin, older than half the apps on his phone.

He saved a frame from his grandmother's video, the one with the stop sign and the mailboxes, and dragged it into the little camera icon in the search bar. The page thought for a moment and then filled with results. The same street. The same man. The same stop sign, in a news story dated three years ago, from a town two states south, in a flood that had been real but had happened long ago and somewhere else. Below that were other copies, other captions, one claiming it was in Europe, one claiming it was last week in a town Ashton had never heard of. The image had been wearing different disasters like costumes.

He called his grandmother. "Did you check where that video came from?" he asked, too fast.

"I don't check things, sweetie, I forward them," she said. "Rosa sent it to me."

"Rosa's flooding is three years old. It's from Georgia."

A pause, the sound of her television in the background. "Well, it could still happen here."

"It could," Ashton said. "But that video isn't it."

He walked her through the search afterward, at her kitchen table, her phone propped against the sugar bowl, and she followed slowly, tapping the camera icon with one finger like she was testing ice. When the old news story came up she leaned close to the screen. "That's my flood," she said. "That's my man on the sign." She laughed, a short, surprised sound. Then she said, quietly, "Rosa's going to feel terrible."

"She'll live," Ashton said. "Send her the search."

At his mother's office that afternoon, filing invoices nobody had asked him to file, he thought about the argument from the night before. His mother managed money for people, and he had once overheard her tell a client that she was bound by something called fiduciary duty, which meant, as far as he could tell, that she was required to put their interests ahead of her own. It had seemed abstract then, a word underpinning a job he didn't want. Now it seemed less abstract. If forwarding a thing was a kind of promise that the thing was real, then everyone with a phone owed everyone else something they mostly never paid.

Hallie texted him a picture at four o'clock, a garrulous chain message, all capitals, claiming a local bridge had collapsed. "Is this real," she wrote, and for once it wasn't a question mark so much as a request. He pasted the image into the search. It came back from a demolition in 2019, a controlled one, charges set, crowds watching from folding chairs. "Old demolition," he sent back. "Not our bridge." She replied with a single heart, then, thirty seconds later, "I almost sent that to my whole team."

He didn't feel righteous about any of it. He had forwarded things before, at fifteen, at sixteen, things that turned out to be staged or stolen or mislabeled, and nobody had taught him to check them either; he had just gotten lucky with a teacher who mentioned it once and a search box that had existed since 2011, waiting. There were still videos he couldn't verify, still images that came back clean and turned out false anyway, still a Thursday he couldn't see into. That evening he texted Elliana that he would visit Sunday instead, after the shift, and asked, as a joke that wasn't entirely one, whether her college offered a class in not believing things.

She wrote back: "It's called everything. Also bring the flood video, I want to see the man on the sign."

He opened the clip one more time before bed and paused it on the mailboxes, the brown water, the man's white knuckles. Somewhere in Georgia, three years ago, he had really held on. Ashton saved the frame again, cleanly this time, and set his phone on the charger, screen still glowing with the search results, the same street repeated six times down the page under six different dates.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The word valedictorian comes from the Latin vale dicere, meaning "to say farewell," which is why the valedictorian gives a farewell speech.
story:
Jayden sat at the kitchen table with the speech draft in front of him and crossed out the first line for the fourth time. "As I stand here today" was gone, "we stand at a threshold" was gone, and "four years ago" had never survived its first minute. His mother had taped the announcement to the refrigerator: Jayden Marsh, valedictorian, ceremony Saturday, eleven o'clock. Every time he went for water he had to look at his own name in her looping handwriting.

Beckett came through the back door without knocking, the way he had since they were nine, and dropped into the chair across from him. "How long is it."

"It isn't, yet. I've got a page of things I've crossed out."

"Read me one of the corpses."

Jayden turned the paper around. Beckett read it in silence, then said, "You wrote 'our journey has only begun.' Twice."

"I know."

"You're going to stand up there and equivocate for eight minutes. 'This is an ending, but also a beginning. We'll never forget, but we must move forward.' You're trying to say two things at once so nobody can argue with either."

Jayden pulled the paper back. "That's what a graduation speech is. It's the genre."

Camryn arrived twenty minutes later with a grocery bag of snacks and no sympathy. She read the draft while eating pretzels, crumbs falling on his crossed-out lines, and when she finished she said, "It's a farewell speech. That's the whole job. Say goodbye to people and mean it."

"That's the part I can't do without sounding corny. Every farewell in every movie, every yearbook page, they all sound the same." He flattened the draft against the table. "I keep thinking there's some angle I'm missing."

Camryn tilted her chair back. "My sister had Ms. Vargas for Latin. She used to go on about word roots. Valedictorian, vale dicere, it means to say farewell. That's why the valedictorian gives the farewell speech." She shrugged. "It's literally the job description. You're the person who says goodbye."

Beckett was already typing on his phone. "She's right. It's Latin. Vale, like in valete, farewell. Dicere, to say." He set the phone down. "So the title isn't about being first in the class. It's about being the one who speaks the goodbye."
