Jayden wrote vale dicere at the top of a clean page. He sat with it while the kitchen clock ticked and his mother's television murmured from the other room. The word had stopped being a trophy somewhere in the last week, somewhere between the award letter and now, and it had started being an assignment: the person who has to find words for a thing nobody has words for. That was different from being the smartest. That was harder.

He tried a line out loud. "We've spent four years on a kind of isthmus, this narrow stretch between childhood and whatever's next, and on Saturday we walk off the end of it."

Camryn made a face. "The isthmus thing is a stretch. Half the gym won't know the word and the other half will think you're showing off."

"She's right," Beckett said. "Cut it. Keep the goodbye part. Don't dress it up."

Jayden crossed it out. Then he crossed out the crossed-out line from before, and the one before that, until the page was turbid with ink, a mess of black lines over words he'd tried to make true and hadn't. He turned to a fresh sheet. At the top he wrote: What do I actually want to say to Beckett? To Camryn? To people I never talked to?

"That's it," Camryn said, reading upside down. "Start there. Names, not nouns."

He wrote Beckett's name. He wrote Camryn's. He wrote the name of a girl from his chemistry lab who had carried his binder when he broke his wrist in eleventh grade, and the name of a boy on the cross-country team who had quit mid-season and whose locker had stood empty like an apology. The page began to fill with particular things, small ones, and none of them felt corny, which was the strange part. The small things were the ones that held.

"Say one out loud," Beckett said. "A real one. Right now, so we can tell you if it dies in the air."

Jayden looked at the list. He looked at the two of them sitting in his kitchen, eating his pretzels, the same as a hundred other afternoons that would stop happening after August. "Saturday," he said, "when I say we're done, I mean we're done with this. Not with each other." He waited, pen still in his hand.

Camryn nodded slowly. Beckett reached across the table and took the last pretzel. "Write that down before you lose your nerve."

Jayden wrote it down.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: 'I-messages', such as 'I felt stuck when the slides came in late', were promoted by psychologist Thomas Gordon in the 1960s as a way to raise problems without blaming.
story:
Stella sat on the outside edge of the merry-go-round with her notebook on her knees, trying to rewrite one sentence before Daphnee arrived. The original sentence was easy: "You ruined the presentation." The slides had come in at eleven the night before, she had stayed up reordering them, and the whole thing had limped. The new sentence was harder. In Ms. Müller's class they had read about a psychologist named Thomas Gordon, who in the 1960s promoted something called "I-messages," lines like "I felt stuck when the slides came in late," meant to raise a problem without blaming. Stella had copied that down. Now she was testing whether she actually believed it.

Her first draft read, "I felt some frustration at certain points." She looked at it and crossed out "certain points," which was the kind of phrase that calcified into nothing the longer you stared at it. Daphnee would hear the softness and understand it as permission to change nothing, and then Stella would have spent her honesty on a counterfeit.

Daphnee came across the wood chips with Angela, both of them carrying iced coffees, and they dropped onto the carousel beside her. Angela had been the one who told Stella to meet at the playground instead of the library, on the grounds that nobody could fight properly in a library. She was right about that, Stella thought, and probably right about more things she hadn't said yet.

"Okay," Daphnee said, unwrapping a straw. "You've got your face on."

"I have notes," Stella said, and immediately regretted "notes," which sounded like a trial exhibit. She turned the notebook toward Daphnee anyway. Daphnee read it, and her shoulders came up around her ears.

"So this is the script," Daphnee said. "You rehearsed."

"It's not a script. It's an I-message. Thomas Gordon, the psychologist, he promoted these in the sixties. 'I felt stuck when the slides came in late.' You start with what happened to you instead of what's wrong with the other person."

"That's so much worse," Daphnee said. "At least 'you ruined it' is honest."

Stella had prepared for this and had still prepared wrong. She had assumed the risk was Daphnee getting angry. Instead Daphnee was hurt, which was different, and the notebook sentence sat between them looking incisive in a way Stella hadn't intended, like a scalpel presented as a gift.

"Here's what I didn't put in the notebook," Stella said. "Two things are true. The slides came in late and it wrecked my night, and you spent your whole weekend on the design while I was at my grandmother's. I left that part out because it felt like softening. But leaving it out isn't kindness, it's just editing you into a villain."

Angela stirred her coffee and said nothing, which Stella suspected was a discipline Angela practiced the way other people practiced piano.

Daphnee was quiet for a moment, turning her straw wrapper into a tight coil. "I thought you'd liked them. The slides. You said the animations were clean."

"They were clean. That's actually part of it. You're good at this, so when you coast, it shows. If you were bad at it I wouldn't bother being mad." Stella heard how that sounded and let it stand, because it was true and because softening it further would have been a third draft, and a third draft was just avoidance with better grammar.

"I didn't coast," Daphnee said. "My dad was in the hospital. I didn't want to tell anyone because it felt like an excuse." She said it flatly, looking at the wood chips, and Stella felt the whole notebook go weightless in her lap. There was no sentence, first person or second, that competed with that.

"I'm sorry," Stella said. "Next time, when something's wrong, I'd rather know early. Even mid-disaster. Even by text at two in the morning."

Angela leaned back on her hands. "For the record, I voted for not doing this at all. I've changed my mind. It went better than the library would have."

"It hasn't gone yet," Daphnee said. She pulled the notebook toward her, took the pen out of Stella's hand, and under the crossed-out drafts wrote, "I'll send slides by Sunday noon, hospital or no hospital." She added her initials, then pushed it back and held out the pen. Stella wrote hers underneath, feeling faintly ridiculous, faintly eight years old, and mostly relieved. On the swings behind them a kid was dragging his feet to stop at the highest point, letting the chain jerk him sideways.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Under the US Fair Labor Standards Act, non-exempt employees must be paid one and a half times their regular rate for hours worked beyond 40 in a workweek.
story:
Claire had told herself the job at Marlowe's would be simple, and for the first three weeks she almost believed it. She bussed tables, rolled silverware into napkins, and memorized the register codes Devyn had scrawled on a receipt for her. Devyn, who had worked there since junior year, called the place a pit, though she said it with no real venom. The only vitriolic voice in the restaurant belonged to the fry cook, who screamed at the dishwasher whenever the tickets piled up, and even that had become weather, something you stood under rather than argued with.

The trouble began with the schedule. Winter break stretched eighteen days across the calendar, and everyone else wanted time off, so Claire said yes. Yes to Tuesday doubles, yes to the Saturday that ran eleven hours because a pipe had burst at the rival diner down the road and their customers came flooding in, hungry and impatient. She did not count the hours. That, she would later understand, was the first mistake, though not the one she thought it was.

She remembered the afternoon Mr. Choi hired her, back in November, when the leaves were still holding on. He had slid a laminated card across the table in the last booth, the one by the window where the sun hit at four o'clock, and said eight twenty-five an hour, cash tips pooled, and she had nodded because everyone nodded. "Read the whole card," he had said, tapping it twice, but a party of eight had come in and he had been pulled away, and she had folded it into her back pocket and, eventually, through some laundering of jeans, lost it.

The paycheck came on a Thursday. She waited until her break to open the envelope, sitting on the milk crates by the walk-in, and that was where the confusion started. Most of her hours were listed at her regular rate, but the last eleven hours of the week showed a different number, higher, and a small code beside it that meant nothing to her. Her first thought, quick and hot, was that Mr. Choi had made an error in her favor, or, stranger, that he was paying some people more for identical work, and she decided she would say nothing and see if it happened again.

It happened again the following week, same structure: forty hours at one rate, then the extra at one and a half times that rate, clean as arithmetic. She was in the back booth after close, under the four o'clock sun that now arrived closer to six, doing the multiplication on a napkin, when Devyn dropped into the seat across from her with two sodas.

"You look like a payroll savant over there," Devyn said. "What are you, doing taxes?"

Claire turned the napkin around so Devyn could see. "The hours past forty in the week. They're at a higher rate. One and a half times the regular rate, exactly. Why? Is it a bonus? Is it favoritism? Because if it's favoritism I didn't ask for it."

Devyn laughed, then saw that Claire was serious, and set her soda down. "It's overtime. It's the law. Hours past forty in a workweek, they have to pay you time and a half. Mr. Choi isn't doing you a favor. He's doing what he has to."

Claire looked at the napkin again, at the neat columns she had drawn, and felt the small humiliation of having constructed a mystery out of a rule. She had been so certain there was a story here, a wrong to be rooted out or a secret to be kept, and instead there was only a law, applied without drama to her eleven extra hours. And yet a thread of uneasiness stayed with her, because she could not shake the memory of the laminated card, the one she had never read. If the law set the floor, what else had been on it, in the fine print she had folded away and lost? Whether the tip pool, or the doubles, or the broken Saturday all sat above that floor or below it, she genuinely did not know, and she disliked not knowing more than she had liked the mystery.

She went to find Mr. Choi while he was counting the drawer. "Can I get another copy of that card from when I was hired?" she asked. "The one with the rates. I want to read the whole thing this time."

He looked at her for a moment, then reached under the register and pulled one from a stack, and slid it across the counter toward her, laminated and stiff under the fluorescent light.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: One mole of an ideal gas takes up about 22.4 litres at 0 degrees Celsius and 1 atmosphere of pressure.
story:
The note from Ms. Adeyemi was folded into Vanessa's quiz so tightly it looked like a pellet, and she had carried it home without opening it, the way you carry something that might burn. The quiz itself sat face down on the kitchen table beside her chemistry textbook, a red 62 bleeding through the paper. She had a retest on Monday. She had the weekend. She had, she told herself, plenty of time, and then she went to the pantry and requisitioned the biggest cardboard box she could find, the one the rice came in, forty by forty by forty centimetres if she measured generously, which she did, twice, with the tape measure from the junk drawer.

The problem she kept getting wrong was problem four. Given 8.4 grams of sodium bicarbonate, calculate the moles of carbon dioxide produced. She could do the first half: divide by molar mass, 84 grams per mole, so 0.10 moles. But the second half asked for volume, and her answer of "0.10 litres" had been circled in red with a question mark so forceful it had torn the paper slightly. She'd argued about it with Marcus after class, briefly, before he got sidetracked by the zeitgeist of the hallway, which today was a rumour about the principal. Marcus thought the volume question was unfair. Vanessa thought it was unfair too, which was different from thinking it was wrong.

Hector came over at four, letting himself in through the back door the way he did, shaking rain off his jacket onto the linoleum. "You're building a fort," he said.

"I'm building a mole."

"Of what?"

"Gas. Carbon dioxide." She pencilled the box's dimensions on its side. Sixty-four thousand cubic centimetres. She knew that much math. She also knew that the number was meaningless until she had something to compare it to, and that the something was in the folded note she still hadn't opened.

She had been avoiding it for a reason. Ms. Adeyemi wrote notes on quizzes only when she suspected the problem wasn't effort. The last note Vanessa had gotten, in October, had said I think you understand this better than your answers show, and Vanessa had not enjoyed how that made her chest feel, so this time she'd decided the note could wait until she'd solved the thing herself. Independence, she called it. Hector called it stalling, but he said it mildly, and sat down, and pulled the textbook toward him with the patience of someone watching a pot that hadn't boiled yet.

The kitchen smelled like the toast she'd abandoned. The gas stove ticked faintly as it cooled. Outside, the rain had softened into something the sycamore could absorb without complaint. Vanessa ran her finger down the reference table in the back of the chapter, past molar masses, past boiling points, down to a small boxed note near the bottom, and stopped.

"Read it out," Hector said.

"One mole of an ideal gas takes up about 22.4 litres at 0 degrees Celsius and 1 atmosphere of pressure." She read it flatly, the way you read a speed limit. Then she read it again, slower, because something had shifted. Not a paragraph of explanation. Not a derivation. Just a fact sitting there in the appendix like a stone in a riverbed, and she had walked past it every time she'd studied, eyes fixed on the flashcards she'd made, on the formulas she'd memorized, on everything except the one plain sentence that made problem four possible.

She did the arithmetic on the back of a receipt. Twenty-two point four litres per mole, times her 0.10 moles from the 8.4 grams, was 2.24 litres. Not 0.10 litres. Two point two four. She looked around the kitchen for something that size and found it: the large saucepan, the one her mother used for soup, filled to its brim once and emptied into the measuring cup in careful cups until the water reached 2.2 litres and slopped a little over. That was it. That was how much gas came out of 8.4 grams of powder, less than a tablespoon of the baking soda sitting in the cabinet three feet from her elbow. She stood there with wet hands, holding a pan of cold water, understanding for the first time that chemistry class had been happening in her kitchen all along, in the box of rice, in the igneous-looking grey counter she'd never once thought about, in the air she was breathing.

She opened the note. Three words, in Ms. Adeyemi's small handwriting: Check the appendix.

Hector laughed so hard he knocked the tape measure off the table, and Vanessa poured the water back into the sink and wrote 2.24 L on the box's side in thick marker, then underneath it, smaller, the whole sentence about 22.4 litres and 0 degrees and one atmosphere, so she'd see it every time she reached for the rice.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: The Seder plate holds maror, bitter herbs such as horseradish, which are eaten to recall the bitterness of slavery in Egypt.
story:
The haggadah sat open on the table like a dare, its pages soft from forty years of thumbs, and Jack's grandfather had said only one thing about it that afternoon: "You're old enough now." Jack had nodded as though he understood what that meant, and now, with the whole family arranged around his grandmother's long table and the candles already lit, he understood it less than ever. His grandfather sat at the far end, hands folded, waiting. Jack's mother poured the first cup of wine, not for drinking yet, and everyone looked at Jack.

He began with Kiddush, the way he had practiced in his bedroom with the door shut, and his voice came out steadier than he expected. His grandmother's china caught the candlelight, and the silver Kiddush cup, the one his grandfather had carried out of a country Jack could barely locate on a map, seemed to burnish itself brighter as Jack raised it. When he finished the blessing, his grandfather gave a small nod, and Jack felt something in his chest unclench.

Jenna sat to his left, a guest at a Seder for the first time in her life. She had come home with him for the break because her own family was scattered across two coasts, and she had offered to bring a dessert and then, upon learning what dinner would involve, a notebook, in which she had written, during Jack's rehearsal that morning, "ask questions, don't be weird about the crackers." She leaned toward him now while his mother refilled glasses and whispered, "Okay, so what's with the plate? Everyone keeps glancing at it like it owes them money."

The Seder plate sat at the center of the table, holding its small ordered mysteries: a shank bone, a roasted egg, a green vegetable, a paste of apples and nuts, and a slice of horseradish root, pale and ragged, that looked like something you would feed a horse. "It's not just a plate," Jack said, keeping his voice low so the table's murmur covered it. "Everything on it stands for something." He touched the edge of the dish. "This one's the maror, bitter herbs. Horseradish. You eat it on purpose, to recall the bitterness of slavery in Egypt." Jenna looked at the horseradish, then at him. "You eat something bitter," she said slowly, "on purpose." "That's the whole idea," Jack said. "You don't skip the bad part. You taste it."

He turned back to the haggadah and led them through the Four Questions, which his youngest cousin recited in a sing-song that wobbled between Hebrew and English, and through the telling of the story, where Jack stumbled once, badly, on a passage about plagues, and his aunt helped him by starting the sentence over loudly from its middle. He noticed his grandfather watching him through all of it, not with criticism, Jack decided, but with attention, which felt nearly the same and entirely different. There had been a Seder two years ago when Jack had refused to come inside until the singing started, had stood on the porch with his headphones in, fifteen and certain that rituals were for people who couldn't think of anything better to do. He remembered his grandfather opening the door anyway, saying nothing, leaving it unlocked. He weighed that memory now against the plate in front of him and could not make them balance.

When the time came for the maror, Jack portioned it out himself, laying the bitter herb onto each person's matzah with the charoset, and when he reached Jenna he gave her a smaller piece, which she noticed. "You're cutting me a break," she said. "Maybe," Jack said. His grandfather, though, took a piece twice the size of anyone else's, held it up briefly as if toasting with it, and ate it without flinching, though his eyes watered and he did not wipe them. Nobody remarked on it. Jenna took a bite of her own, made a sound like a kettle starting, and drank the water Jack pushed toward her. "That's genuinely awful," she said when she could speak. "Yes," said Jack's grandmother, from the far end, with something that was almost a laugh.

His cousin asked why they couldn't just tell the story without the horseradish, since everyone already knew the story, and Jack started to answer and then stopped, because his grandfather had raised one finger, not sharply, just enough. "We could," his grandfather said. "Some people do." And then he put his hand flat on the table and looked at Jack, offering him the sentence back.

Jack thought about the two versions of the night that existed in his head. In one, ceremony was decoration, the kind of thing that made a meal bombastic and long when it could be short and honest, and he had believed in that version on the porch two years ago with real conviction. In the other, the one assembling itself in front of him now, the horseradish did something the words couldn't do alone; the burning in the mouth was a kind of knowledge, and his grandfather's watering eyes were not weakness but a man tasting an old country on purpose. Jack could not prove which version was truer. He suspected they were both true, and that the plate, the long table, the unlocked door, and his own presence at the head of it were all an argument for the second version that he would have to keep choosing, year after year, without certainty.

"Because knowing isn't the same as tasting," Jack said to his cousin, and to the table, and possibly to the porch. He held up his own piece of maror. "You have to taste it." His grandfather nodded, once, and reached for the matzah.

They ate. Jenna drank more water. Somewhere between the second and third cup, the singing started, and Jack listened for the porch door, but he was already inside.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird, a black cat peers over Kahlo's shoulder, usually interpreted as a symbol of bad luck and death.
story:
Luke had spread his materials across the kitchen table like a detective who believed a crime had been committed in oils: two library books on Frida Kahlo, a printed reproduction of Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird, a legal pad, and a bag of tortilla chips he was using as thinking fuel. The assignment from Ms. Müller was due Monday. Formal analysis, she had written on the board, underlined twice. Colour, composition, symbolism. She had also said, in a voice that suggested she knew exactly what she was doing to them, that she would accept no paragraph beginning with "I feel like."

His mother drifted through the kitchen, glanced at the thorn necklace piercing the painted flesh, and said, "That's cheerful," and drifted out again with her tea.

The problem was that Luke could look at the painting all afternoon and still not know what to say about it. The woman in the picture stared straight out at him, level and unbothered, a monkey tugging at the thorns and a hummingbird, dead, hanging from the necklace like a pendant. Behind her, leaves in every green the printer could manage, and a butterfly or two in her hair. He wrote "green: a lot of it" on the legal pad, looked at it, and crossed it out.

Eliana arrived at four with her own books, because Ms. Müller had assigned the same painting to half the class and Eliana believed, correctly, that they were both doomed. She dropped into the chair across from him and pulled the reproduction toward her.

"Okay," she said, tapping the image with one finger. "Inventory first. There's the monkey. There's the hummingbird, obviously, it's in the title. There's a dragonfly, or that might be a butterfly, there's two of them. And there's a bug on her shoulder that I refuse to identify."

"A cat," Luke said, and stopped.

There was a cat. A black cat, its whole head visible over the woman's left shoulder, watching the viewer with round yellow eyes, and somehow Luke had not seen it until he said it, which felt like a magic trick performed on him by his own mouth. He leaned in. The cat was not hiding. It sat between the tropical leaves as if it had every right to be there, and once Luke saw it, it was nearly all he could see.

"When did you notice that?" Eliana demanded, as though he had been holding out on her.

"Just now. I've been staring at this for an hour and I just now saw the cat."

"That's a whole animal, Luke. That is not a small detail. That is a mammal."

He found it in one of the library books, in a caption so brief it was almost embarrassed: the black cat peering over Kahlo's shoulder is usually interpreted as a symbol of bad luck and death. He read it aloud and sat back. Eliana chewed a chip and considered the cat.

"So she put a death cat next to her own head," she said. "On purpose. And then painted herself looking at us like it's a Tuesday."

That was the hinge, Luke thought, or something like a hinge. He collated what he had: the dead hummingbird, the thorns drawing blood at the throat, the cat that meant what it meant, and then, against all of it, that absolutely steady gaze. The composition was doing something strange. Everything at the edges pointed inward, toward the face, the thorns, the animal mess of symbols, and the face refused all of it. It was almost funny, the way the painting kept handing you doom and the woman kept declining the delivery.

"It's like a list of everything wrong," he said, "and a face saying none of it is the point." He wrote that down, then worried it was too neat. Too neat was its own kind of lie.

Eliana proposed a theory involving the monkey as loyalty and the cat as the fate she carried around casually, the way Luke carried his cracked phone. Luke proposed that they were both guessing. She proposed that guessing with evidence was called analysis, and guessing without it was called her ex-boyfriend's opinion of jazz.

He tried a paragraph. He wrote about the greens crowding the figure, the flat frontal symmetry, the small blood-red points at the thorn's punctures drawing the eye exactly where the necklace bit. Then he wrote that the cat and the hummingbird, read together, made a kind of double announcement, and the calm face answered it. He underlined nothing twice. He left a margin note asking whether the butterfly in her hair meant resurrection or just decoration, because he had found three books disagreeing and it seemed more honest to say so than to pretend the reading was settled. Some of it was probably happenstance. Maybe Kahlo liked the cat. Maybe she liked bugs.

"Is that tenable?" Eliana asked, reading over his shoulder. "The last part."

"It's honest," Luke said. "That's different from tenable but I'll take it."

His mother passed through again, looked at the cat, looked at Luke, and said, "He's judging your essay." Luke pulled the notebook out of her reach and kept writing.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: In a 1999 study, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh found that people liked a partner more when the partner subtly mimicked their posture and movements.
story:
The mock interviews were scheduled for Friday afternoon, which gave Arianna four days to stop being the kind of person who looked at her shoes when a question had more than one part. She wanted the job at the marina snack bar more than she had admitted to anyone, including herself, because admitting it meant admitting what it would cost to lose it. Ms. Lombardi, who ran the camp's leadership program and had agreed to adjudicate the mock interviews, kept a clipboard and a folding chair under the pavilion awning, and the whole thing had an official air that made Arianna's throat tighten just walking past.

Tea found the magazine first. She was lying on the floor of Cabin 6 with her feet up on Raphael's duffel bag, flipping through a water-warped copy of a psychology periodical someone had left in the lost and found, narrating anything that sounded scandalous. "Listen to this," she said. "In 1999, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh found that people liked a partner more when the partner subtly mimicked their posture and movements." She looked up. "So if you copy how someone's sitting, they like you better."

"That sounds like cheating," Arianna said.

"It sounds like science," said Raphael, who considered himself a connoisseur of manipulation techniques, mostly from watching his older brothers talk their way out of chores. He sat up. "It's not lying. You're just, like, agreeing with your body."

Arianna took the magazine and read the sentence twice. She was not sure the two ideas could live together: be honest and clear, and also arrange your body to be liked. Her mother had told her once that a good answer is worth more than a good impression, but her mother had also ironed Arianna's shirt before every school concert, so the advice came from someone who cared about both. She decided to test it, which felt more honest than deciding to believe it.

On Friday she sat across from Ms. Lombardi in the folding chair, and she noticed that Ms. Lombardi leaned forward when she asked about reliability, elbows on her knees. Arianna hesitated, then leaned forward too, matching the angle, and answered about the summer she had watered a neighbour's garden every morning for six weeks. Ms. Lombardi's expression softened almost imperceptibly, the way a window softens when rain stops. Arianna kept going, mirroring the tilt of the other woman's head when the questions turned to handling a difficult customer, and at the end Ms. Lombardi said it was the strongest interview of the afternoon and that her eye contact had been remarkable.

Arianna walked back to the cabin feeling lighter and also slightly uneasy, the way you feel after winning a game whose rules you only partly understand. Tea wanted every detail. "Did you do the thing? The mimicry thing?"

"I tried it," Arianna said. She sat down on the porch step. "I don't know if it worked or if she just liked my answers. That's the part I can't tell. It might be both at the same time." Raphael argued that the distinction didn't matter, that results were results, and Tea argued that it absolutely mattered, that being liked for a reason you manufactured was different from being liked for who you were. Arianna listened to them go back and forth, garrulous and certain in opposite directions, and found she agreed with each of them about half the time.

The real interview came on the second-to-last day of camp, at the marina office with its smell of sunscreen and outboard motors. The manager was a broad woman in a red visor who asked standard questions from a laminated sheet. Arianna gave her clear answers, the ones she had practiced, and she kept her eyes steady. Then, midway through a question about weekends, she noticed that the manager had crossed her legs, right over left, in the same moment Arianna had, and had tilted her chin at nearly the same angle. Arianna felt her face warm. She could not decide whether the woman was doing it on purpose, or whether it was happening underneath both of them, unchosen, the way a conversation finds its own rhythm.

"You're hired," the manager said, standing to shake her hand. "You remind me of myself at sixteen. Uncross your legs, though. You're going to need to be able to get up fast around here."

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: The electric field between charged plates points from the positive plate toward the negative plate, the direction a positive charge would be pushed.
story:
The worksheet had a diagram of two parallel plates, one marked positive and one marked negative, and Mia drew her arrows from the negative plate toward the positive one because that was how she had drawn them in her notes last week, and last week nobody had corrected her. She was on her third arrow when Lucca leaned across the bench, chin on his fist, and looked at her paper the way people look at a car parked across two spaces.

"Which way would a proton go in there?" he asked.

"A proton's positive, so it goes toward the negative plate. Obviously." She said it fast, because the word obviously usually bought her a second to think.

"Then your arrows say protons go backward."

The lab was loud with the sound of twelve people not understanding electricity, so there was room for her to equivocate. She said something about how maybe the arrows meant electron flow, or convention, or how the book drew it, which was the kind of sentence that sounds like knowledge but is really just fog. Lucca kept looking at her. On the next bench, Adria was highlighting her own worksheet in three colors, which was either deep understanding or elaborate camouflage, and Mia could not tell which from where she sat.

"Draw a proton," Lucca said. "Just draw it. Little circle, plus sign."

She drew it halfway between the plates, and then she drew a second one touching the positive plate, because that was the only way she could force the question to be concrete instead of a matter of opinion. The positive plate would push it, she thought. Positive pushes positive. And that meant it would drift across the gap toward the negative plate, all the way, because there was nothing else in between except the field itself. She looked at her arrows, which pointed the other way, and crossed them out one at a time, pressing hard enough that the paper went slightly gray. The field pointed from the positive plate toward the negative plate. The direction a positive charge would be pushed. She hadn't known that five minutes ago, and now she couldn't understand how she'd ever believed anything else, which is the particular embarrassment of being right after being wrong.

"Better," Lucca said. He turned back to his own paper, where his arrows had been correct from the start, and Mia felt a small flare of injustice about that, since he had clearly guessed.

The problem at the bottom of the worksheet wanted the field strength at a point three quarters of the way toward the negative plate, and it gave the potential difference and the plate separation, so the whole thing reduced to dividing one by the other, which should have taken forty seconds. It took Mia ten minutes because she kept checking whether the answer should be negative, whether direction lived inside the number or outside it, whether a field that pushed a proton leftward was a different quantity from one that pushed it rightward or just the same quantity wearing a sign. Adria leaned over her shoulder, saw the crossed-out arrows, and raised an eyebrow.

"You had it backwards too," Mia said, "last Thursday. I watched you."

"That was the old me," Adria said, unbothered, and went back to her highlighting.

The twist, when it came, was quiet. Ms. Papadopoulos moved through the room collecting the worksheets, and at Mia's bench she stopped, tilted her head at the crossed-out arrows, and then looked at her own master copy, the one she'd photocopied from the department folder. She looked at it for longer than a teacher usually looks at anything. "Huh," she said. On the printed diagram, the sample arrows in the margin, the ones the whole class had copied as gospel, pointed from the negative plate toward the positive plate, the wrong way, and had apparently done so for years, through four teachers and, by her expression's math, possibly a decade of students.

"Does everyone get the marks back, then?" Lucca asked.

"Everyone who fixed it gets the marks. Everyone who copied it gets to fix it." Ms. Papadopoulos set the master sheet face down on the bench, as if it were something that had died. "I'm not claiming complicity in a diagram I didn't draw. But I am the one who photocopied it, so."

Mia sat with her corrected arrows and the number she'd computed, the one that was a magnitude wearing a direction she could now justify out loud, proton by proton, if anyone asked. It occurred to her that the perspicacious move would have been to question the handout from the beginning, the way Lucca had questioned her, without caring whose authority was attached to the arrows. It also occurred to her that she'd only arrived at the truth because Lucca couldn't draw, or wouldn't, and had needed her diagram to copy the layout from, and so had looked at it hard enough to notice it was wrong. She decided not to mention that part.

"Next year someone should check the folder," Adria said, capping her third highlighter.

"Next year someone will photocopy it again," Lucca said.

Ms. Papadopoulos picked up the stack of worksheets, tapped them square against the bench, and looked one more time at the face-down master sheet before dropping it into her bag. "Erase one arrow for me," she told Mia. "I want to see if you can still do it when nobody's wrong about it but you."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: In Judaism, the closest relatives of the person who died sit shiva, a mourning period of seven days that begins after the burial; the Hebrew word shiva means seven.
story:
The hospital corridor smelled of floor wax and something faintly sweet that Eli could not name and did not want to name. His grandfather had been moved out of the room by the time Eli arrived, and so the goodbye happened in a hallway, beside a vending machine that hummed like a trapped insect, where his mother stood holding the dead man's glasses in her fist as if she had forgotten she was holding them. Eli had run the whole way from the bus stop. He had missed the last hour, and the missing of it sat in his chest like a stone he had swallowed.

"You can still go in," his mother said. "He's still there. For a little while."

Eli went in. The bed had been straightened, the tubes taken away, and his grandfather looked strangely available, like a photograph of himself that no one had asked for. Eli touched his grandfather's hand, which was cool in a way that hands were not supposed to be, and said nothing, because everything he thought of saying sounded like something from a movie. Outside the door he could hear his aunt on the phone, her voice climbing and breaking, and a nurse asking someone, gently, to please sit down.

For two days the apartment filled and emptied like a tide. His father, who could usually be debilitated by nothing worse than a bad back, moved through the rooms slowly, bent over something invisible. Relatives Eli half recognized brought containers of food and stood in the kitchen arguing softly about whether the funeral should be Wednesday or Thursday, which was really an argument about something else, though nobody said what. Eli answered the door, carried chairs, and found that grief in a small apartment was mostly logistics.

On the morning after the burial, Maram texted him: can I come by. I don't know what you're supposed to do. bring anything? Eli stood in the hallway holding the phone and realized he did not know either. Nobody had handed him a rulebook. He had watched his aunts cover the mirrors, had watched his father tear his shirt, and had understood these things the way you understand weather, by standing in it.

When Maram arrived, he was carrying a plastic bag with a fruit tart in it, which he held out at arm's length like a passport at a border. "I didn't know," he said. "My mom said food, but my mom also said flowers, and then she said maybe not flowers, and then she made me a list and lost the list."

Eli took the tart. "Food's right," he said. "There's like a whole table of it, my grandmother keeps pointing at it. We're sitting shiva. It means seven. Seven days, and it started after the burial, so this is the first one."

"Shiva," Maram repeated, careful with it, the way you'd handle a word you didn't want to drop. "Seven days of what, exactly? Sitting?"

"Mostly sitting. People come, you say stuff, or you don't say stuff. There's a thing where you don't really greet them, they just come in. My cousin told me last night and then went morose on the couch for an hour." Eli shrugged. "I'm making it sound like a biome, like there's a whole ecosystem and I'm doing field notes. I actually don't totally know what I'm doing."

Maram looked at the covered mirrors, the low stools his parents were sitting on, the tart now joining four other desserts on the table. Adeline was already there, sitting cross-legged by the window, having apparently figured out the whole system hours ago. She raised a hand in greeting without getting up, which Eli later realized was the correct gesture, and which Maram copied immediately, badly, standing.

They sat for a while without talking, which turned out to be its own kind of doing something. Eli's grandmother brought them plates they hadn't asked for. Outside, someone's car alarm went off and stopped, went off and stopped, and inside nobody stirred. Maram ate a piece of tart with the concentration of a boy defusing something.

"Can I ask something dumb," Maram said finally. "Do you believe in it? The seven days. Like it does something."

Eli considered the plate in front of him. "I think it doesn't matter if I believe in it," he said. "It's doing it anyway. Yesterday I couldn't sit still, and today sitting still is the whole assignment, and somehow that's, I don't know, easier and worse at the same time." He stopped, aware he had said more than he meant to. Adeline was watching him from the window with her chin on her knees.

His father looked over from the low stool and, for the first time in three days, almost smiled.

"Come back tomorrow," Eli said to Maram. "We still have six."

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A meta-analysis combines the results of many studies on the same question to estimate the overall effect more precisely than any single study can.
story:
Jonathan spread the two photocopies across the kitchen table, weighting their corners with the salt cellar and his mother's mug, which still held an inch of cold coffee. Mr. Munro had assigned a critical review: one question, two articles, and the instruction that he take neither at face value. The question Jonathan had chosen, somewhat against his will, was whether later school start times actually improved adolescent sleep. The first article said yes, emphatically. The second said the gains evaporated within weeks, that adolescents simply sequestered the extra hour in front of screens.

His father passed through to refill his own mug and glanced at the pages. "One of them's wrong," he said, which was exactly the assumption Jonathan was trying to dismantle.

"That's the thing," Jonathan said. "I don't think either of them is lying. They measured different schools for different lengths of time."

His father carried his coffee out, and Jonathan turned back to the table. The yes-article followed two schools for a year. The no-article followed eight schools for six weeks. He wrote in the margin of his notebook, small, so it wouldn't look like a conclusion: the year-long study saw more, but of less; the six-week study saw less, but of more. Then he crossed that out because it sounded clever and meant almost nothing, and cleverness was what Mr. Munro had warned them about on the first day, holding up a sample essay and calling it a machine for disguising opinion as analysis.

He texted Maryam, who had chosen the same question because she dozed through first period and considered it a personal matter. She replied with a screenshot and one line: did you find the meta-analysis yet. He typed back, what's that.

She called him. "It's a study of studies," she said, mouth half full of something. "A meta-analysis combines the results of many studies on the same question to estimate the overall effect more precisely than any single study can. There's one from a couple of years ago, like forty studies. Your two are probably in it."

He found it while she was still describing her own essay, which she claimed was going to be a virulent takedown of the early schedule, though she had written only the title. The meta-analysis pooled the forty studies and reported a modest overall effect, real but smaller than the yes-article claimed and more durable than the no-article allowed. Jonathan sat with that for a moment. It was unsatisfying the way true things often were, neither side vindicated, both sides reduced.

Devon arrived at four to work on his own review, which was about class size, and immediately tried to sequester the best chair by draping his jacket over it before taking off his shoes. He read over Jonathan's half-formed draft, the paragraph where Jonathan had written that the yes-article treated its two schools as if they stood for every school, a kind of metonymy, one part answering for the whole.

"That word's showing off," Devon said.

"It's the right word."

"It's still showing off." Devon tapped the page. "But this part's good, where you say the six-week window can't see what the year can. Keep that. Cut the part where you sound like a lawyer."

Jonathan cut the part where he sounded like a lawyer. The new draft said what the two articles saw, what each was positioned to miss, and where the pooled estimate fell between them. Then, at the bottom, he added a sentence he was not sure Mr. Munro would like: that even the meta-analysis could only describe the average adolescent, and that he, Jonathan, lying awake at midnight regardless of when school started, was beginning to suspect the average adolescent did not exist. He looked at the sentence for a long time. It was either the most honest thing in the essay or an excuse for not deciding. He left it in.

When his father came through again on his way to bed, the table was still covered, the salt cellar still holding down page four, and Jonathan was reading the pooled study a third time with a pencil he wasn't using.

"Verdict?" his father asked.

"There is no verdict," Jonathan said. "There's an estimate."

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Commencement means "beginning"; the word was used for graduation ceremonies because graduates begin a new status, such as being a bachelor or master.
story:
The party was in Jayden's backyard, which meant the fairy lights came out once a year and one strand always died halfway along the fence, so that the lawn had a bright half and a dark half, and everyone kept drifting toward the bright half out of instinct. Avery stood at the border with a warm can of ginger ale and watched her classmates behave like people who had already left. They were leaving, technically. Half of them had dorm assignments and packing lists and group chats that had quietly renamed themselves after their destination cities.

Avery had skipped a grade, which was why she was sixteen tonight and graduating with people who could all drive and had turned eighteen in stages over the spring. It hadn't felt strange until now. Now it felt like being handed a departure notice for a flight she'd booked a year early. Mr. Zhu, who had taught her twentieth-century history and lived two doors down, was by the food table in a Hawaiian shirt, talking to Jayden's mother about property taxes. He raised his cup at Avery. She raised her ginger ale back.

"Your speech was good," Lochlan said, materializing beside her. He'd been in her English class since the skipping had thrown her there. "The part about the library carpet."

"I liked the library carpet."

"I know. That's why it was good." He took the dead strand of lights personally; she could see him looking at it. "You're not sad about the school, though. You're sad about something else."

She didn't answer that, because it was true and because the answer was embarrassing: she was sad about starting. Everyone kept saying begin, begin, the whole world leaning forward, and she felt like the only person at the party standing still. In September she'd be the youngest person in every room again, and she'd have to do the work of being taken seriously all over from the beginning, the slow enfranchisement of a sixteen-year-old among adults who assumed she was someone's little sister visiting campus.

"Nobody told me graduating would feel like this," she said. "They show you the gowns and the caps. They don't mention the part where you stand in a backyard at ten at night feeling like a funeral just happened."

"Funeral." Lochlan considered it. "You do know what commencement means."

"A ceremony. Walk, speech, tassel."

"It means beginning. That's the whole point of the word. They called graduation that because the graduates begin a new status. Like becoming a bachelor or a master." He said it flatly, the way he corrected citations. "So technically you just attended a beginning and spent it mourning."

Avery looked at him, then at the bright half of the lawn, where Jayden was teaching someone's younger cousin a dance that involved a lot of arm-waving. She tried to hold both things at once, the grief and the correction, and found they didn't cancel. The word was true and so was the feeling. Maybe the feeling needed the word, actually; maybe that was why they'd named it that, so that the people walking across stages in heavy robes would have something to push against.

"I owe you a reparations cupcake for that," she said. "I ate yours at the after-ceremony thing. I was emotional. I wasn't accountable for my actions."

"You're accountable now. Chocolate, no frosting."

They went inside, where the kitchen had gone quiescent after the earlier rush, empty platters still out, a single intact cupcake under plastic wrap. Mr. Zhu was at the sink rinsing glasses, uninvited and undeterred. He glanced at the cupcake changing hands.

"Splitting it," Avery said. "As a legal settlement."

"Fair restitution," said Mr. Zhu, and went back to the glasses.

They ate it in halves on the back steps, the dark half of the yard in front of them now, which turned out to be where you could see the stars. Lochlan named a constellation and got it wrong, and she let it stand, because she'd had enough correcting for one night. In September he'd be at a school four hours away, and she'd be somewhere else entirely, and both of those facts sat in her chest next to the word beginning, which she decided she was allowed to hold like a coin with two faces.

"Text me when you're the youngest person in a lecture hall," Lochlan said.

"Text me when you fail astronomy."

He held out the last piece of cupcake, and she took it.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: The phrase 'rule of thirds' was first written down by John Thomas Smith in his 1797 book Remarks on Rural Scenery.
story:
The contest entries had to be on the table by the front desk before the library closed at six, and at four Sophie still had no horizon. Her watercolor was of a fishing town she had never visited, assembled from a photograph in a book about the Atlantic coast, and the sea refused to sit where she wanted it. Zachary had the desk beside hers in the community room, three tables pushed together under the tall windows, and he kept leaning over to look.

"Put the horizon a third of the way down," he said. "Abigael told me that last week. It makes everything look right."

Sophie dipped her brush and held it above the paper without touching. "Who made that a rule?" she said. "Somebody had to decide it worked. Somebody had to write it down first."

"Probably it's just, like, ancient. The Greeks or whoever."

Mr. Fernando, the librarian who ran the Friday sessions, came by with the sign-up sheet for the wall space. He was not an art teacher and did not pretend to be one; he mostly found people the books they needed and left them alone. Sophie raised her hand as though he were still a teacher from her primary school, then lowered it, embarrassed, and just asked. Was there a book that said where the rule about thirds came from?

He looked at the clock over the doorway, then walked with her to the reference shelves. The catalog terminal took two searches. He pulled a heavy reproduction volume and set it open on the study carrel, and while Sophie read, he went back to shelve returns. Zachary drifted over and read over her shoulder, chewing the end of a pen.

John Thomas Smith. Remarks on Rural Scenery, 1797. The phrase "rule of thirds" had been first written down there, in that book, by that man. Not ancient, not Greek. A specific person, in a specific year, looking at rivers and sky and deciding how to divide them. Sophie copied the title into her notebook, and the pen wobbled because she was still holding the wet brush in her other hand, and a bead of water fell onto the page and bloomed under the words.

"So it's one guy's opinion from two hundred years ago," Zachary said. "That's kind of great. That means you can break it."

Sophie went back to the community room. Abigael was there now, laying out ink drawings of whales for her own entry, careful pelagic shapes that looked like they belonged to deep water, and Sophie stood behind her for a minute before saying anything. Abigael painted the ocean as though she had swum in it, which Sophie had not, and the honesty of that difference bothered her more than the horizon did.

She tried the horizon a third of the way down. It did look right. The sky opened, the harbor settled, the little boats found a place to float, and for a moment she felt the ease of doing what she was told, the way following a recipe allays the fear of cooking for guests. Then she turned the brush around and swept the waterline nearly to the top of the sheet, so that the sea filled everything and the town stood small at the bottom edge, cramped and pressed upon, the way the photograph had actually felt to her, like a place holding its breath against the water.

"It's wrong," Zachary said. "I mean it's good, but it's wrong by the rule."

"It's wrong by one man in 1797," Sophie said. "He wrote it down first. He didn't make it true."

Abigael looked up from her whales. "You can't know it's better," she said. "You just know you like it."

"That's the part I can't fix," Sophie said. She signed the corner, which was the only deadline that mattered now, and carried the sheet to the front desk with both hands flat underneath it, like a server, like a pilgrim. The clock said 5:41. She set it down, and the librarian on duty wrote her name on the entry list, and behind her the doors opened and a cold gust came through the lobby and lifted one dry corner of the paper, just slightly, before it lay still.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: In Canada outside Quebec, a typical paycheque shows deductions for income tax, Canada Pension Plan contributions and Employment Insurance premiums; Quebec uses its own pension and parental insurance plans.
story:
The staff room at Marcello's smelled of burnt espresso and dish soap, and Nicolas sat at the corner table with his first paycheque flattened in front of him like evidence. He had worked eleven shifts since the middle of June, bussing tables and running food, and the number at the top of the stub was smaller than the number he had calculated in his head on the walk over.

"Six hundred and forty," said Aron, who had come in for his own cheque and stayed. "That's not bad."

"That's the net," Nicolas said. "Look at the gross. Eight-twelve." He slid the paper across the table, and Aron bent over it with the interest of someone reading another country's currency.

Nicolas pointed at the lines going down the stub. Federal income tax, then provincial. Then a line marked CPP and another marked EI, each with its own smaller amount subtracted, so that by the bottom of the column almost a fifth of his pay had gone elsewhere. He had known, vaguely, that taxes existed the way weather existed, but seeing the arithmetic applied to his own eleven shifts made the abstraction suddenly personal.

"I never even looked at mine," Aron said. "I just check the deposit amount."

He pulled out his phone and opened a photo of his own stub, from the pizza place in Gatineau where he'd worked the previous summer, living with his aunt. Nicolas leaned in expecting the same lines. Instead there were abbreviations he didn't recognize, and no CPP at all.

"Yours is Quebec," Nicolas said. "Mine says Canada Pension Plan."

"Mine says QPP," Aron said. "And something called QPIP. I think the P is parental."

"So we paid into different things for the same kind of job." Nicolas set the phone down and looked at both documents side by side, his paper stub and Aron's photo, two versions of the same transaction. In the rest of Canada, he understood now, a paycheque like his showed income tax, CPP and EI. Quebec ran its own pension and its own parental insurance plan instead. He turned this over without deciding whether it struck him as sensible or merely complicated.

"You two are going to sit there all afternoon?" Ms. Cho had come in for her break, the woman who ran the cash and had worked at Marcello's longer than anyone. She nodded at the stubs with something close to amusement.

"Nicolas is doing accounting," Aron said.

"I'm counting," Nicolas said. "Different thing."

She left them to it and went to make her tea, and the two of them went back to the table where a party of six was finishing. When Nicolas cleared their plates he also collected the bill folder, and as he carried it to the cash he noticed the itemized receipt: the food total, then a line for the five percent federal sales tax, then a separate line for the provincial tax, then the combined amount. Tax appeared twice on his paycheque, before he was paid, and again on the receipt, after. He rang the table through, watched the register do its arithmetic, and counted out their change.

His mother had asked him last week how much he expected to clear by September, and he had given her the gross figure, an insouciant number, tossed out with the confidence of someone who had never read a pay stub. He could still hear himself saying it. He had assumed the money would simply arrive, whole, and that his contribution to tuition and the bus pass would be straightforward math. Now the math had more lines in it, and each line took a share before the share he'd promised her.

That evening, after the dinner rush, he sat with his father at the kitchen table doing the family's tax return for the first time. His father had always done it alone, but this year he pushed the forms toward Nicolas and drank his tea while Nicolas read. On the return, the income from Marcello's appeared exactly as the stubs had summed it, and the deductions appeared again, on different lines, in a different vocabulary. Federal and provincial amounts. Boxes that referred to contributions and premiums already taken. The system seemed to want him to reconcile the story twice, once per cheque and once per year.

"You're frowning," his father said.

"I'm trying to figure out if I actually paid this or if they're just telling me I did."

"Both," his father said, and that was the whole of his explanation.

Nicolas filled in the boxes slowly, checking each number against the stubs Aron had helped him sort into a pile. At one point his father suggested, as fathers do, that he claim his bus pass, and Nicolas wrote the amount on the correct line and felt the total shift, minutely, in his favour. It was not much. It was something. The next morning at Marcello's, Laura came in for coffee before her shift at the bookstore, and Nicolas slid his stub across the table to her without saying anything, just to see whether she'd read it all the way down.

She read it all the way down. "What's QPIP?" she asked.

"Ask Aron," Nicolas said. "He's from the other side of the river."

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: TinEye, a reverse image search engine launched in 2008, can sort results with the oldest first, helping find when an image first appeared online.
story:
The photo arrived in the group chat at 7:14 in the morning: a stadium half drowned, water to the third row of seats, a rescue boat idling near the pitcher's mound. Randy had sent it with the caption "THIS IS HAPPENING RIGHT NOW 20 MINUTES FROM SCHOOL." Ashley stared at it on the bus, thumb hovering over the forward arrow. Two hundred people followed her repost account, and last month she had been the first in the whole school to post the chemistry lab fire. Being first felt like a kind of currency, and she was aware of spending it carefully.

She forwarded it to Eamon instead of to everyone, because Eamon never shared anything without reading the whole thread first, a habit that used to strike her as timid and now struck her as something else. "You going to post it?" she typed. His answer came back in under a minute: "Hold on. That looks familiar."

In homeroom, Ms. Littlechild was taking attendance and telling everyone that afternoon sports were cancelled pending the storm, which so far consisted of a gray sky and a wind that moved the flagpole rope against the pole with a small metallic tapping. Ashley sat near the window and pulled up the photo again. Rain was genuinely forecast. Nothing about the picture contradicted the forecast, and that was the trap she could feel herself wanting to walk into: the photo fit the day, so the day must have produced the photo.

Eamon slid into the seat beside her, phone already out. "You know how you can search a picture instead of words?" he said. "Reverse image search. There's a site called TinEye. It's been around forever, since 2008, my cousin used it in college." He pasted the photo's URL into the search bar and a page of results came up, dozens of copies of the same image scattered across the internet. "The trick is the sort," he said, and clicked a dropdown. "Oldest first."

The results reordered themselves. The earliest match was dated years before, on a forum about hurricane damage in a state neither of them lived in. Ashley scrolled down the list and watched the same water, the same boat, the same drowned outfield accumulate date after date, none of them this week. The "breaking" photo had been breaking for nearly a decade. "So Randy got played," she said. "Or Randy is playing us." Eamon shrugged. The two possibilities sat next to each other and neither of them could be resolved from a phone screen, which bothered her more than the false photo did.

She thought about her repost account, the way a certain kind of follower counted on her, and about the English unit they had just finished, where Ms. Littlechild had taught them the word metonymy, the crown for the king, the press for the journalists, and had asked them what it meant that people said "the internet says" as if the internet were one voice with one mouth. Ashley had written a paragraph about that and gotten an A minus. The A minus now seemed generous toward her, since she had been one of those mouths, forwarding a flooded stadium as if a picture were a sentence with a date built into it.

She opened the chat and started typing, deleted it, started again. What she wanted to write was "this is fake," which was more certainty than she had. What was true was narrower: the picture was real, the flood was real, and it had happened years ago somewhere else. She had been sensitized, recently and uncomfortably, to how easily a true image could be borrowed to certify a false moment, and she noticed that the noticing itself was new, that a month ago she would have posted it and gone to first period feeling fast and useful. Sometering in her had been quiescent until now, some habit of asking where a thing came from, and it had woken up at an inconvenient time, after she had already built a small reputation on speed.

She typed: "Photo is old. TinEye, sort oldest first, it's from years ago. Don't share." Then she added the link to the results page so anyone could check, because a claim without the trail was just another thing to forward. She pressed send before she could soften it. In the window, the first drops of the actual rain touched the glass, small and scattered, nothing like a flood yet.

Randy replied with a single question mark, and then, a minute later: "wait really." Ashley held the phone so Eamon could see it, and the two of them watched the typing indicator pulse under Randy's name while the rain got steadier against the window and Ms. Littlechild, at the front, read out the last name on her list.

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: When a candidate's lead is smaller than the margin of error, the poll cannot say with confidence who is ahead, but that does not mean the race is exactly tied.
story:
The line outside Jefferson Middle School stretched past the bike racks and into the parking lot, and Nolan stood in it with a clipboard he was too young to need. He was sixteen, ineligible to vote for two more years, and had volunteered as a student observer because Ms. Clarke-Williams had said it would look good on applications and because, honestly, November had been settling over him like a gray coat of ennui that even the campaign signs along Route 9, bright as they were, could not puncture. His job was to count, quietly, and stay out of the way.

Emaan had come to vote with his father and found Nolan by the doors. "You should see the office downtown," Emaan said, hands jammed in his jacket pockets. "Marley's been there since six. She thinks we're winning. The new poll has us up by two."

"Two points," Nolan said. "What's the margin of error?"

Emaan shrugged, but the question followed him inside, and Nolan watched through the gym doors as the voting machines blinked and accepted ballots one by one. An old man at the check-in table grew querulous about his address change, his voice rising until a poll worker in a blue vest came over and calmed him with the patience of someone who had done this many times before. Nolan marked the incident in his tally, though it belonged to no column he had been given.

At noon Marley appeared, energized and cold, wearing the campaign's sticker like a medal. "We're up two," she announced to Nolan and to Emaan, who had come back out. "It's in the paper."

"The paper says it's within the margin of error," Emaan said. "Four points. So it's a tie, basically."

"It's not a tie," Marley said. "Two means two. We're ahead."

Nolan had spent enough evenings half-listening to his mother's phone bank calls, enough afternoons skimming the statistics chapter Ms. Clarke-Williams had assigned for no reason he could then name, to feel the shape of something between them. "Can I say something?" he asked, and when they let him, he said it carefully, because he was assembling it even as he spoke. "When the lead is smaller than the margin of error, the poll can't say with confidence who's ahead. That doesn't mean the race is exactly tied."

Marley frowned. Emaan turned the words over.

"So nobody's ahead," Emaan said.

"No. It means the poll doesn't know. It's not allowed to tell you." Nolan looked at his clipboard, at the meaningless tally of a morning's small conflicts. "We could be ahead. They could be. The poll just can't say which."

For a moment the two of them stood in the cold with the line shuffling past, and Nolan thought about how badly each of them wanted the number to mean something, wanted the arithmetic to suture the gap between what they hoped and what they could know. He understood the wanting because he shared it. "But we're still up two on paper," Marley said, quieter now. "That's better than being down two."

"That's true," Emaan conceded, and it seemed to Nolan that this was the real work, not the arguing but the holding of both things at once: the number was something, and the number was not enough, and neither of those cancelled the other.

The afternoon thinned the line, and by four o'clock the gym had emptied enough that Nolan could hear the voting machines' small confirming chirps, one, then another, like birds counting to themselves. Ms. Clarke-Williams stopped by on her way out of her own precinct to see how he was managing, and he told her about the morning's count, the old man, the machine tally, the argument. "Good," she said. "Most people never learn that a poll is a guess wearing a suit." Then she was gone, and Nolan went back to the doors.

Marley and Emaan came by again near closing, carrying coffee they didn't offer to share, and stood beside him watching the last voters walk in under the sodium lights. "So what do we do now?" Marley asked, meaning the campaign, the night, the waiting. Nolan looked down the emptying parking lot, at the people who had come all day to make the only count that didn't need a margin of error, and said, "We watch this one." Behind them, the machine chirped again.

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: Transport costs shrink the gains from comparative advantage, and if shipping a good costs more than the difference in production costs, trading it no longer pays.
story:
Rachel had taped the sign to the front of the table herself, block letters gone slightly crooked in the heat: LEMONADE, $1.50, COLD. The crookedness bothered her less than the arithmetic did. Two dollars for lemons at the corner store, four dollars at the farmer's market across town, and Livia kept insisting the market lemons were worth the trip because they were cheaper per lemon, somehow, in a way she couldn't quite say. Rachel wanted to be able to say it. That was the whole problem. She had a quiz Monday in Ms. Sultani's class on comparative advantage, and the textbook chapter had turned turgid in her hands halfway through, paragraphs of jargon she couldn't metabolize into anything she could actually use at a folding table on a Saturday.

"Okay," she said, dumping ice into the pitcher. "Say I can squeeze twelve lemons in an hour. Say you can squeeze eight. I'm better at squeezing. But I'm also better at hauling, and you're terrible at hauling. So it makes sense for me to haul and you to squeeze, even though I'm better at both. That's comparative advantage. We both gain if we each do the thing we're least bad at."

Livia frowned at the pitcher. "Then we should go get the market lemons. They're fifty cents cheaper a bag, and you said cheaper was the point."

"The point is both sides gaining," Rachel said, but even as she said it, a doubt opened under the words, quiet as a crack in ice. Markus had been on the bench behind them for twenty minutes, nursing his cup, and now he leaned forward.

"You're forgetting the bus," he said. "Two seventy-five each way. That's five fifty to bring back a bag of lemons that costs fifty cents less than the ones four blocks from here." He turned his cup slowly on its rim. "You'd spend eleven times the saving just moving the lemons."

Rachel looked at him, then at the corner store, visible from the stand, its awning sagging in the sun. The numbers arranged themselves with an almost physical click. The difference in what the lemons cost was the gain, and the bus fare ate the gain whole and then kept eating. There was a sentence in the textbook about this, she was almost sure, something she had read at eleven at night and not understood, and now it was standing in front of her wearing a bus pass.

"So the trade only pays if it costs less to move the thing than the difference in what it costs to make it," she said slowly. "Otherwise the cheaper lemons aren't cheaper. The shipping eats the advantage." She reached for her phone to text herself the sentence before it dissolved, and Ms. Sultani appeared at the table with her sunglasses pushed up into her hair, holding out a crumpled two.

Markus watched Rachel take the money and count out change, and he thought, not for the first time, that she treated the stand like an exam and exams like stands. When Ms. Sultani asked how business was, Rachel told her about the lemon problem, the whole thing, bus fare and comparative advantage and the difference between production costs, laying it out the way you'd lay out a proof. Ms. Sultani listened, sipped, and said only, "So you decided against the trip," and Rachel said yes, and Ms. Sultani said, "Good. Most people never count the distance," and walked off down the block with her cup.

Livia had gone quiet during all this, refilling the ice tray, and Markus understood the quiet. The stand had been her idea. The market trip had been her idea too, an adventure attached to a reason, and now the reason had been dismantled in public by a girl with a phone and a boy with a bus schedule. There was something bathos-shaped about it, the grand principle of nations enriching each other through trade, resolved at a folding table over thirty lemons and a roll of paper cups. He didn't say any of that. He said, "There's still the plain ones at the corner store. I'll walk with you if you want."

They walked, and Rachel let Markus carry the bag even though she was stronger, which was, she noticed, its own small division of labor, though not the kind that would appear on any quiz. The store's lemons were smaller and duller than the market's would have been. She paid two dollars. On the way back she tried to hold both truths at once: the math was right, the trip wasn't worth it, and yet something had been lost anyway, a morning across town, the better fruit, the version of the plan that had Livia in it laughing. Gains and costs, stacked on the same scale, and the scale refusing to balance neatly.

When they got back, Livia had sold four cups and had drawn a new sign in marker, FREE ADVICE WITH EVERY LEMONADE, ECONOMICS OUR SPECIALTY. Rachel laughed, and then didn't, because Livia was smiling in the way that meant it was half a joke. The ice had gone thin in the pitcher, water blooming pale through the yellow.

"So Monday," Livia said, capping the marker. "When she asks you to explain why two countries both gain. You going to tell them about lemons on a bus?"

"I'm going to tell them trade only pays if moving the goods costs less than the difference in making them," Rachel said. "And then I'm going to say I learned it standing right here." She picked up the pitcher and poured the last cup, mostly water now, and handed it across the table to Livia.

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: Ireland's Great Famine began in 1845 when potato blight struck a population that relied heavily on one potato variety, the Lumper, whose lack of genetic variety left it vulnerable.
story:
The petition had forty-one signatures by third period, which Avery counted twice under her desk while Mr. Doyle drew river systems on the board. Forty-one people wanted the lot behind the hardware store turned into a community garden, and thirty-three of them, according to the comment sheet Rayna had taped inside her notebook, wanted potatoes. "They're foolproof," one neighbor had written. "Nobody can kill a potato."

"They're cheap and they fill you up," Rayna said now, leaning across the aisle as the bell hadn't rung yet. "If we're growing food for the food pantry, we should grow the thing that feeds the most people per dollar. That's just math."

Avery turned the comment sheet over. On the back she had copied, in her own handwriting, the budget Jiya had worked out: seed, soil, fence, water. Potatoes took the smallest line. Everything else, the beans, the squash, the chard, added up like a debt. "It's not just math, though," she said. "It's also what happens the year the math stops working."

Mr. Doyle, who had been pretending not to listen, pulled a chair around and sat on it backwards, which he did when he wanted to seem like not a teacher. "You're in the middle of a real argument," he said. "Monoculture versus resilience. Historians argue about it with actual graveyards." Then he stood up and went back to his rivers, which was his way of saying the argument belonged to them.

It was Jiya, scrolling her phone at lunch, who found the graveyard. "Okay, this is grim," she said, pushing the screen across the table toward Avery. "Ireland. The Great Famine started in 1845." She kept reading, slower, like the words were heavier than the article's font suggested. "Potato blight struck a population that relied heavily on one potato variety. The Lumper. It didn't have genetic variety, so basically all of it was vulnerable. One variety, one blight, and that was it."

Avery remembered, then, her grandfather's garden, the summer she was nine. Two long rows of the same bean, seed saved in a coffee can and planted again every year because his mother had done it that way and her mother before. In August a rust had come through and taken both rows in a week, and he had stood at the fence not swearing, which was worse, just looking, and the next spring he planted six kinds of bean and saved seed from all of them, and grumbled about the paperwork of it until September. She had thought it was stubbornness. She had thought a garden was a place where you got to do things your own way.

She said none of this out loud. What she said was, "We could split it. Half the beds in Lumper-style logic, one reliable crop, because reliability is what the pantry actually asked us for. The other half in my grandfather's logic, six things, so a bad year takes a bad year and not the whole garden." She heard how unhinged it sounded to say "Lumper-style logic" to a boy from the hardware store, and she kept going anyway. "It costs more. I don't know how much more yet."

"That's not a compromise, that's doing both projects badly with one budget," Rayna said, but she said it quietly, and she took the comment sheet back and read it again, all forty-one names, as if the names themselves might tell her which project the signatures had actually been for. Jiya started a new column in the budget called "the half that fails," and wrote a number in it, and crossed the number out, and wrote a smaller one.

Volition, Avery thought, was the word for what she wanted the garden to be: not a charity that neighbors received but a thing they chose and therefore owned.
