A garden could emancipate people from the food bank line or it could just move the line behind a fence; whether their half-measure was tenable depended on a summer they hadn't lived yet, a blight they couldn't predict, a committee that hadn't met. She looked at the two budgets side by side, the small one and the split one, and understood that the small one would pass tonight, at the community center, by a comfortable margin, and that the split one might not pass at all.

At the meeting, the vote went to the split plan. Not because anyone quoted Ireland, but because an old man in the back row stood up and said, "My father grew beans the way your grandfather grew beans," looking directly at Avery as though he had been at that fence too, and the room shifted. It was tenacious and probably doomed and fully funded for exactly one year. Afterward, carrying the sign-in sheet to her mother's car, Avery passed the empty lot and stopped. Someone had already tilled a strip along the north edge, unsanctioned, unexplained, a single straight line of turned earth, and planted in it, she could see even in the dusk, row after row of one identical seedling, all the way to the fence.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex, published in 1949, contains the line usually translated as 'one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman', arguing that society shapes womanhood.
story:
The bookshop smelled of dust and coffee gone cold, and Ella had claimed the corner table an hour before anyone else arrived, spreading her battered copy of Jane Eyre across it like evidence at a trial. Beside it sat a photocopied page from Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex, published in 1949, which Ms. He had slid across the counter last Tuesday with the words, "You asked the right question. Here's someone who asked it first." Ella had underlined the line "one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman" so hard the pen had gone through the paper.

Ryland arrived first, shaking rain off his jacket and dropping into the chair opposite her. "So what's this emergency session? Karen said you'd gone full detective."

"Close reading club," Ella said. "Attendance: two." She pushed the novel toward him, open to the passage where Jane agrees to marry Rochester. "Read that and tell me she's making a free choice."

Ryland read, mouthing slightly the way he did when he was concentrating. "She sounds pretty happy to me. 'My husband is not to me what he is to the world.'" He looked up. "That's romantic. That's, like, the most romantic thing anyone's ever said."

"That's the problem," Ella said, and tapped the Beauvoir page. "Either it's her choice, or it's what her world trained her to want. It can't be both."

"Why not?"

The question sat there while Karen came in, stomping, buying a biscuit she didn't need, and pulling up a third chair. "Am I late for the revolution?"

"We're stuck on whether Jane Eyre counts as a feminist text," Ryland said. "Ella says marrying Rochester is capitulation. I say it's true love. Karen, tie-breaker."

Karen broke her biscuit in half with surgical care. "Ms. He would say you're both asking the question wrong." She nodded toward the counter, where the owner was pricing a box of paperbacks with a pencil stub. "Ask her."

Ella carried the bookshop's one complete Beauvoir over to the counter, 1949 stamped inside the cover, and Ms. He read the marked line without being told which one. "The French is better," Ms. He said. "'On ne naît pas femme.' But the idea survives translation. Society shapes womanhood, whatever language you complain in." She handed it back. "Don't quote it at people like a hammer. Use it like a lens. There's a difference."

Walking back to the table, Ella caught herself doing the thing she hated in essays, the thing her teacher circled in red: treating every question as having a verdict at the end. Marxist lens, feminist lens, grade, move on. But Ryland had asked why it couldn't be both, and she didn't have an answer, and the not-having was starting to feel less like failure and more like the actual assignment.

"Okay," she said, sitting down. "New system. We take the passage apart twice." She held up her left hand. "Marxist: Jane has nothing. No family, no money, no name that matters. Rochester owns the house, the dog, the ward, and, functionally, her job. Her choices are circumscribed before she makes them. Marriage is the only door in the room." She held up her right hand. "Feminist: the world told Jane from childhood that to be a woman was to be quiet, small, grateful. The wanting itself might be trained. Beauvoir's whole point is that you're not born with it, you become it, and you can't fully see the shaping from inside."

"So it's hopeless," Ryland said, not sadly, more like he'd been handed a fascinating piece of bad news.

"It's homeostasis," Karen said around her biscuit. "Sorry, bio ruined me. The system corrects itself. You push on it, it pushes back to the same shape. Jane pushes by loving on her own terms, and the terms were still given to her."

Ella wrote both of those sentences down, then stopped, pen hovering. "But she leaves him. When she finds out about Bertha, she walks out with nothing, into actual hunger, because staying would cost her the one thing she claims as hers. If her wants were entirely trained, where does that come from?"

"Self-preservation isn't exactly a personality," Karen said.

"It's not extrinsic, though. It's not something the world paid her to want." Ella heard herself and laughed. "I'm arguing with myself now. Out loud. In a bookshop."

"That's just called thinking," Ryland said. "Apparently it's loud."

They worked until the shop's closing bell, filling the margins with arrows, crossing them out, drawing better ones. Ella never got her verdict. What she got was a page where Jane's choice was marked once as conditioned and once as brave, both underlinings left standing, and a note to herself at the bottom that read, possibly both, possibly neither, ask again after rereading. Ms. He passed their table on her way to lock the till and glanced down at the double-marked paragraph.

"Good," she said. "You left the wound open." She turned off half the lights, and Ella copied one more quotation into her notebook while she still could, by the glow of the front window, the rain outside making small silver rings on the glass.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: In Texas v. Johnson (1989), the Supreme Court ruled 5-4 that burning the American flag as a political protest is protected symbolic speech.
story:
Anthony spread the case brief across his grandfather's kitchen table, which was still scattered with a fly-tying vise and a coffee can of fishing lures. He had been assigned the harder side of the mock Supreme Court: he had to argue against flag burning as protected speech, in front of Ms. Fischer's civics class, even though his first instinct was that people should be allowed to burn whatever they owned. The assignment sheet called it an exercise in advocacy. It felt more like being handed someone else's conscience and told to wear it.

"You're doing homework at my table on a Saturday," his grandfather said, coming in from the garage with a thermos. He was a phlegmatic man, slow to alarm and slower to praise, and Anthony had learned to read his approval in smaller signals, like an extra slice of toast appearing beside his plate.

"Mock court," Anthony said. "I have to argue that flag burning isn't protected speech. Except I keep finding out it is. Texas v. Johnson, 1989. That's the whole problem."

His grandfather sat down and turned the brief toward himself without asking. "That one," he said. "The Supreme Court ruled five to four that burning the American flag as a political protest is protected symbolic speech." He slid the page back. "You know what a five to four means, don't you. One justice different and your side wins."

Anthony had known the number, of course; it was printed in the second paragraph. But he hadn't felt it until now, sitting in this kitchen with the smell of WD-40 and the radio murmuring a ballgame his grandfather wasn't watching. Five to four meant the country itself was nearly split down the middle, which meant the argument he was about to make was not a straw man he could knock down in rehearsal. It was the argument of four sitting justices, and half of everyone he would ever meet.

He called Nickolas from the porch, where the yard gave out into a scruffy savanna of uncut grass gone gold in the late summer heat. Nickolas had drawn the opposite side, the easy side, the side both of them actually believed, and he proselytized about it shamelessly over the phone, going on about free expression as if Anthony hadn't heard of it. "You should just throw the argument," Nickolas said. "Everyone will know you don't mean it."

"That's not the assignment." Anthony watched a hawk turn slow circles over the grass. "Ms. Fischer said the point is to make the strongest case for the position you draw. If I sandbag it, I'm just insulting the people who actually hold it."

"Then hold it. Actually hold it. Go find out why."

Anthony went back inside and read the dissents. He read them twice, then a third time in the overstuffed chair by the window, while his grandfather cooked eggs and onions and said nothing. The dissenting justices worried that flag burning was conduct, not speech, and that a nation needed certain shared symbols to hold itself together. Anthony didn't agree, exactly, but he began to see the shape of the worry, the way you can see the logic in a relative's politics once you stop caricaturing them. He drafted his opening argument on the back of a grocery receipt.

Madilyn came over on Sunday to drill him. She played the bench, firing questions the way she imagined the real justices might, and she was merciless about it. When Anthony argued that the flag was a unique symbol of national unity, she leaned forward and said, "Unique how? Symbolic speech is symbolic speech." He stumbled, regrouped, and tried again, and the second version was better, and the third version was better than that. He was honest with her about the part he couldn't fix: his conclusion kept sounding like someone else's certainty wearing his voice.

On Monday morning he stood at the front of the classroom with his notes face down on the podium, because he had decided he could not argue this from paper. He made the case for limiting symbolic speech, and he made it as well as he could, and when Madilyn-as-justice pressed him he conceded the point about how close the vote had been, five to four, one justice apart, because pretending otherwise would have been a weaker argument, not a stronger one. Afterward Ms. Fischer asked him, quietly, which side he actually believed. Anthony said, "The other one. But I understand mine better now," and watched her write something in her grade book, the pen moving in small, unhurried strokes, like a man casting a line across still water.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Raising the temperature for an exothermic reaction decreases its equilibrium constant, while raising it for an endothermic reaction increases the constant.
story:
The garage smelled of cut grass and two-stroke fuel, because Mr. Kerr's lawnmower lived in the middle of it and Mr. Kerr himself had gone inside, leaving Lucas and Farah and Maxwell to the card table wedged between the workbench and the wall. Lucas had his textbook open to the chapter on equilibrium, and a quiz hung over all of them like weather.

"Five dollars," Maxwell said, tapping the table. "Five says the reaction speeds up no matter which direction the heat goes. Heat is heat."

"You're being belligerent about a thing you haven't read," Farah said. She didn't look up from her phone.

"I'm being confident. There's a difference."

Lucas wanted the five dollars, or told himself he did. What he wanted more was to stop guessing. All semester he'd answered equilibrium questions by feel, choosing whichever direction seemed like the question wanted him to choose, and his marks had the flat, mediocre look of a coin toss. Tomorrow's quiz was supposed to be the one that mattered.

Farah turned her phone around. "Look at this. My cousin sent it from her notes. A data table." Lucas read it over her shoulder: a reaction, marked exothermic, with equilibrium constants listed at three temperatures. At 25 degrees the K was large. At 45 it was smaller. At 65 it was smaller still. He read the numbers twice, because they went the wrong way, or the way nobody had told him they'd go.

"That can't be right," Maxwell said. "Higher temperature, more product. That's just how it works."

"Look at the column again," Lucas said. "It falls. The K falls the whole way down."

"So the table's wrong."

But the table wasn't the only thing in the room. Mr. Kerr had come back out for a rag, and while he wiped his hands Lucas asked him, carefully, whether heating something always pushed it toward more product. Mr. Kerr said he hadn't done chemistry since he was their age, that he was the wrong man to ask, and went on wiping. That was the whole of his help, and Lucas felt a small detente settle in his own chest anyway, because at least now the question belonged only to them.

He copied the table into his notebook. Then, underneath it, he drew the same reaction running backwards, and wrote endothermic beside the arrow, and sat with the two drawings a long moment. If K fell as the temperature rose for the exothermic one, then turning it around made the constant climb as the temperature rose. Raising the temperature for an exothermic reaction decreased the equilibrium constant; raising it for an endothermic reaction increased it. He said the whole thing out loud, slowly, and Farah nodded along, and Maxwell pulled the notebook toward himself to check the arithmetic, which was Maxwell's way of conceding without conceding.

"It's called Le Chatelier's principle," Farah said. "The shift part, anyway. The K part is what he figured out."

Lucas took out his phone and typed a message to his brother, who had finished this course two years ago: does K change with temp or does it stay fixed. The reply came back a minute later: depends which way the heat goes. exo falls, endo rises. why. Lucas typed why do you think and then deleted it, because the answer was already in his notebook in his own handwriting, and a confirmed thing felt different from a borrowed thing. He put the phone face down on the table.

Maxwell slid a crumpled five across the table without being asked. "Rematch after the quiz."

"After the quiz," Lucas said, and folded the bill once and put it in his shirt pocket, where it sat stiffly against his chest while Farah read out practice problems and the mower ticked as it cooled and the numbers in his notebook went on falling, all the way down the page.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Need-blind admission means a college decides whom to admit without considering whether the applicant can afford to pay; many US colleges are instead need-aware.
story:
The tour group gathered under an oak whose roots had cracked the brick path, and Aaron stood at the back with his hands in his pockets, counting the buildings the guide named as though the number might tell him something. He had applied to this college eleven weeks ago. The email would come, his father kept saying, when it came. The guide, a senior in a polo shirt, spread her arms toward the library and called the campus munificent, generous beyond what students expected, and a mother near the front wrote that down.

Graham had come on the tour too, because their mothers had arranged the drive together, and he kept leaning over to whisper judgments about the tour guide's cadence, the quality of the dining hall smell drifting from the east quad. Graham had a trust set up for him and a list of seven colleges, all of them places where, as he put it, the money part had already been handled years ago. Aaron had a list of five, a work savings of eleven hundred dollars, and a father who had sat at the kitchen table in February with the tax documents spread out like a losing hand of cards.

In the student center they were released for twenty minutes with vouchers for coffee. Saif, whom Aaron knew from physics class and who had turned up on the same tour by coincidence, claimed a table by the window and opened his laptop. "I've been making a spreadsheet," Saif said, turning it so Aaron could see. Columns ran across the screen: deadlines, test scores, and one column headed simply money.

"What's that column?" Aaron asked.

"That's whether they're need-blind or need-aware," Saif said. "Need-blind admission means a college decides whom to admit without looking at whether you can afford to pay." He tapped a cell shaded pale yellow. "This one's not. They're need-aware. They can look at your finances when they decide." He scrolled, and the column shifted between two colors like weather.

"So they know before they say yes," Aaron said slowly, "whether the yes costs them anything."

"They're not hiding it. Most places in the country are need-aware. Only some can afford not to be." Saif said it without bitterness, the way he reported lab results, and turned the laptop back toward himself. Graham, arriving with three cookies balanced on a napkin, asked what they were looking at, and Saif explained again, and Graham nodded and said his counselor had never mentioned any of it, which Aaron supposed was the point. Graham's counselor had never needed to.

They walked the quad after that, the three of them trailing the group, and Aaron found he was doing arithmetic without meaning to. The college whose email he awaited was in the pale yellow rows. It was possible, he understood now, that his file had been read twice: once as a student and once as a bill. He could not decide whether that made the waiting worse or simply more honest. Saif argued that knowing the rules was better than guessing at them, even when the rules were not in your favor. Graham argued that the whole system equivocated, calling itself about merit in the brochures while keeping one eye on the ledger. Both of them, Aaron thought, were describing the same building from different sides.

That night, in the guest room at Graham's house where they were staying until the morning drive home, Aaron wrote to his father, because calling felt too large. He typed: "Found out something on the tour. Some colleges admit people without looking at whether they can pay. That's called need-blind. A lot of others are need-aware, which means they do look. The one I'm waiting on is the second kind. I'm not sure yet what I think about that. Saif says it's just information. I keep imagining a room where my folder sits in a stack and someone opens it and sees the financial aid form before they see my essay. Or after. I don't know which order would be better." He read it over, deleted the last sentence, and then put it back.

The reply came while he was brushing his teeth, a single line from his father: "Either way, we'll figure it out. That's not the part I'm worried about." Aaron stood with the phone glowing in his hand and felt some of the foreboding he had carried through the whole tour loosen, not vanish but loosen, like a knot worked partway free by fingers. Graham was already asleep in the other bed, one arm hanging toward the floor. Aaron set an alarm for the drive home, put the phone face down on the nightstand, and watched the ceiling fan turn until the shadows stopped seeming like anything at all.

At breakfast the next morning, the phone buzzed once against the table between the cereal bowls, and Graham looked up and said, "Are you going to check that?"

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: Affirming the consequent is a logical fallacy: from 'if P then Q' and 'Q', concluding 'P'. Living in San Diego means living in California, but living in California does not mean living in San Diego.
story:
Mr. Gauthier wrote "If P then Q" on the whiteboard, then beneath it, "Q," and asked the class what followed. Maxime copied the letters into his notebook without much thought, because his mind was still down the hall in the office where, that morning, the vice principal had told him to wait outside while Jimmy was questioned about the missing cash box from the café fundraiser. Jimmy had come out pale, holding the late slip he'd been given like it was evidence against him.

Mr. Gauthier set them working in pairs. Dane, across the shared desk, wrote slowly, chewing his pen. "Okay," he said, "if it rained, the lawn is wet. The lawn is wet. So it rained." From the next table Jimmy leaned back in his chair and said, "Sprinkler." Dane looked at his own sentence for a second, then said, "Right. That's affirming the consequent," and drew a line through his conclusion.

Maxime had biology next period, an exam on the immune system he had not studied for, and the words were already mixing in his head, antigens the body learns to recognize and attack, premises the mind tests and accepts. He wrote the fallacy's shape in the margin of his philosophy notes: from "if P then Q" and "Q," you cannot conclude "P." Around them other pairs argued their examples out loud. A girl near the window said, "Living in San Diego means living in California, but living in California does not mean living in San Diego," and Mr. Gauthier nodded and asked her to try the reverse, and she got tangled, and half the class laughed kindly.

Maxime did not laugh. He was drawing an arrow under his notes, because the shape had snagged on something. The vice principal this morning, through the door he'd left ajar: if someone took the cash box, they would have been near the office at lunch. Jimmy was near the office at lunch. The vice principal's voice had been flat and certain, and Maxime had believed it himself until now, sitting here with the letters on the board. He ruminated over it, turning the argument around the way Mr. Gauthier kept telling them to, and then he reached over and tapped Jimmy's arm and asked, quietly, why he had been near the office at lunch.

"To hand in my course change form," Jimmy said. "I've been trying to switch out of foods all month."

"Did you hand it in?"

"It's still in my bag. The office was closed for the meeting about the money."

When the bell rang, Maxime walked with him toward biology. He kept hearing the sprinkler in his head. He had watched the vice principal build a clean tower out of two true statements and one that didn't follow, and he had almost climbed it himself, which was the part that bothered him most. At the same time he could see the other side of it: the school had a hundred and sixty dollars missing, a parent committee demanding answers, and a boy who was the only person anyone had placed near the office. Demanding more than that felt like a luxury to people who had to answer to the committee by Friday.

After last period, Maxime went back to the office. He had written what he wanted to say on a page torn from his philosophy notebook, and now he stood in front of the vice principal's desk while the man finished typing a reply to what looked, from the length and the tone of the opening line, like a scathing email from the committee. "I'm not saying Jimmy didn't take it," Maxime said once the typing stopped. "I'm saying you don't know that he did. Your argument is: if he took it, he was near the office. He was near the office. So he took it. But the form is the sprinkler." He put the course change form on the desk, taken from Jimmy's bag with Jimmy watching, both of them nervous about it. "He was there for this. Somebody else could have been there for the box. Or nobody, if it was moved or lost. I can't prove he's innocent. I can only show the conclusion doesn't come out of what you've got."

The vice principal looked at the form, then at the clock, then at Maxime. He said the committee would want something regardless, that a school couldn't run on reasonable doubt alone, and Maxime said maybe not, but it also couldn't run on the other thing, and neither of them said the name for it. The vice principal pulled the incident file toward him across the desk, opened it, and squared the pages. "I'll look again," he said. "Sit down. Tell me exactly what Jimmy did between twelve and twelve fifteen."

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In 1982 Helmut Kohl replaced Helmut Schmidt as German chancellor through a constructive vote of no confidence, the only time the procedure has succeeded at the federal level.
story:
The debate packet had seemed simple at first: argue that a presidential system is more stable than a parliamentary one. Naomi had underlined the word stable three times before second period and then sat in the library during lunch trying to find out what it actually meant, because the more she read, the less sure she became.

Zakaria slid into the chair across from her and stole a corn chip off her tray. "You look like a woman who has discovered her whole case is made of paper."

"It's made of one example," Naomi said. "The United States. Fixed terms, separation of powers, nobody can just yank a president out midstream. That's stability. That's the entire argument."

"Except impeachment exists."

"Impeachment basically never works. That's my point."

Zakaria spun her pen in a lazy circle. "So find the other side's weakness and hammer it. That's debate. You don't have to believe it."

But that was the problem, and she knew it even before she could say it out loud. She could compartmentalize the parts of herself, the girl who wanted to win the round on Saturday and the girl who wanted to know whether any of it was true, but the wall between them kept thinning the longer she read. She turned back to her laptop and typed the search she'd been circling for twenty minutes: chancellor replaced without election.

The result came up immediately, and she read it twice, then a third time. "Zakaria. Look at this."

He leaned over, chewing. In 1982, Helmut Kohl replaced Helmut Schmidt as German chancellor through a constructive vote of no confidence. It was the only time the procedure had ever succeeded at the federal level. The page sat there, plain and unbothered, like it hadn't just knocked over her whole case.

"So they swapped leaders," Zakaria said. "No election, no crisis, just a vote inside the parliament."

"That's the part that ruins me," Naomi said. "I was going to argue that changing leaders midstream is instability. But look at it from the other direction. The Americans had Watergate and years of a paralyzed presidency, and the Germans got a new chancellor in a single afternoon. The vote, the handover, done. Which one is actually the stable system?"

"You're asking the wrong friend. I'm on your side of the resolution. In theory. In a compartmentalized way."

She laughed despite herself, and then Ms. Castillo, who supervised the library on Thursdays, stopped by their table on her way past with a cart of returns. "You two look like you're fighting about something that matters."

"Debate resolution," Naomi said. "Whether presidential systems are more stable than parliamentary ones. I'm supposed to argue yes, and I just found a thing that makes me think maybe no, and I have to give the speech on Saturday anyway."

Ms. Castillo stacked two books on the cart and considered the screen without touching it. "What's the thing?"

Naomi told her, keeping it short. In 1982, Kohl replaced Schmidt as chancellor through a constructive vote of no confidence, the only time the procedure has succeeded at the federal level. Saying it out loud, she heard how strange and clean it sounded, a whole country's leadership changed without a single ballot cast by a single voter.

"That's interesting," Ms. Castillo said. "I'll be curious what you do with it." And she rolled the cart toward the biography section, which was the most useful thing she could have done, because it left Naomi alone with the problem.

She spent the evening with Nelly at the coffee shop near school, index cards spread between two hot chocolates, trying to build the affirmative case anyway. Nelly was practical about it. "Every system dumps costs on somebody. Like an externality. The American system buys predictability and pays for it with a president nobody can remove. The German system buys flexibility and pays for it with parties toppling their own leaders. Pick which cost you'd rather live with."

"That's not an answer, though. That's just a fancier way of saying it depends."

"Everything depends. That's not a flaw in the argument, that's the argument."

Naomi turned the Kohl card over in her fingers. On the back she had written, then crossed out, then rewritten: a doctrine that can't bend is worse than a procedure that bends once. She'd been trying not to sound doctrinaire about stability, trying to hold both pictures at once, the fixed term and the afternoon handover, without flattening either one.

At Saturday's round, in a classroom that smelled of whiteboard marker, she stood up for the affirmative and made the case for fixed terms, cleanly, with the evidence she had. During cross-examination, the boy from the other school asked whether parliamentary systems could remove a failed leader faster than a presidential one, and she felt the two halves of her week come together.

"They can," she said. "In 1982, Helmut Kohl replaced Helmut Schmidt as German chancellor through a constructive vote of no confidence. It's the only time the procedure has succeeded at the federal level. So yes, it happened once, in one country, in four decades of that republic. Whether one afternoon in Bonn proves the whole system works better, I honestly don't know yet." The judge's pen stopped moving, and the boy across from her tilted his head, and Naomi set the index card down on the desk.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Delayed-onset muscle soreness usually peaks 24 to 72 hours after an unfamiliar or intense workout, not right after it.
story:
Nathan climbed out of bed on Tuesday and nearly went back down, because his thighs refused the stairs. Saturday had been the first real practice, forty minutes of lunges and hill sprints with a new club that trained at the park, and he had walked home that evening feeling triumphant, even smug. He had told Lexie at school on Monday that he was fine, better than fine, and she had given him a look he hadn't understood until now, standing in his hallway gripping the banister. By Wednesday he could sit down only by lowering himself in stages, like a man twice his age, and the walk to the park that afternoon took him twice as long as usual.

Lexie was already there, looping the gravel path in her worn trainers, and she slowed when she saw him coming. "You're walking like a question mark," she said. He lowered himself onto the bench beside the water fountain and told her the strange sequence of it, how nothing had hurt on Saturday night, how Sunday had been fine, how Monday he had bounced through the halls, and how Tuesday had arrived like a debt collector. Lexie stretched her calf against the bench and nodded as though he had confirmed something she had suspected for a while.

"That's the pattern," she said. "It's called delayed-onset muscle soreness. It peaks twenty-four to seventy-two hours after a workout that's new or harder than usual. Not right after." She said it simply, the way she said most things, and then she was quiet while Nathan turned it over. He had assumed pain was a receipt, handed over immediately, proof of work done. Instead it arrived late, in installments, on a schedule nobody had explained to him, which meant his whole sense of what his body could handle was built on bad information.

He took out his phone and opened the notes app. If the soreness peaked on the second or third day, then a hard session on Saturday meant Sunday and Monday were when his legs actually needed mercy, not Saturday night when he felt invincible. He started sketching a week: warm-up drills before anything hard, one genuine rest day, an easier day after each intense one. Lexie leaned over his shoulder and pointed at Thursday, where he had stacked sprints again. "You're being intransigent about Thursday," she said. "You've decided it's a sprint day and no evidence will move you." He argued for a minute, then dragged the session down to a jog and felt, obscurely, like he was conceding something important.

Mr. Rahimi passed on his evening walk, as he did most days, and paused at the bench. He was a neighbour who had run marathons decades ago and now walked the loop with the unhurried dignity of a man who had made his peace with slower distances. He asked about the club, and Nathan explained his new plan, the warm-ups, the rest day, the logic of spacing hard efforts so the worst of the soreness landed on days the schedule could absorb. Mr. Rahimi listened all the way through, which few adults did, and then said only, "The plan is the easy part. Keeping it when you feel good is the hard part." Then he continued around the loop, and Nathan watched him go and did not entirely understand what he meant.

He understood on Friday. The program said easy jog, so he jogged the loop at a pace that felt almost embarrassing, doing his warm-up drills by the picnic tables where Kalli from his class was sprawled with a book, sunglasses on, utterly indifferent to his knee raises. She glanced up once and told him he looked like a man auditioning for a very specific crime. He laughed and kept going, and his legs, to his surprise, carried the joke easily.

By Sunday, the rest day, he felt better than he had all month. He had followed the plan exactly, and now the plan told him to do nothing, and the nothing sat badly, like a reparation offered to a body that no longer felt wronged. The morning was cool and bright, the park's grass still wet, and the hill where they did sprints stood empty and inviting at the far end of the field. He had done all this work, he reasoned, stacking discipline upon discipline, precisely so that a morning like this one could mean something.

He laced his shoes and walked out onto the grass, the whole plan folded away in his phone, and stood at the bottom of the hill. "One," he said out loud, to nobody, to the empty field, and started up.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: Germany uses a constructive vote of no confidence: the Bundestag can remove a chancellor only by electing a successor in the same vote.
story:
The mock parliament was scheduled for two o'clock in the city hall chamber, and by quarter past one the folding tables still had no name cards. Nicholas stacked them in alphabetical order while Mikhail argued with the printer cable and Daniella read out riding names she had invented on the bus, some of them florid enough that even she laughed: Grandview Riverside, Old Mill Flats, Harbourlight. Mr. Costa, who had booked the room and then mostly stayed near the coffee urn, said only that the local rotary club needed the chamber by four, so whatever they were going to break, they should break it efficiently.

They had drawn countries from a coffee mug. Nicholas was the designated constitutional nerd, which meant he had spent two weeks building comparison charts nobody had read: how a president is elected directly and serves a fixed term, how a prime minister emerges from a parliament and can fall when it stops supporting him. Daniella drew Germany and immediately declared herself chancellor. Mikhail drew a presidential republic and spent the morning insisting his president could not be touched by anything short of impeachment, which he pronounced with mock thunder. The friction between them had been useful right up until it stopped being an argument and started being a grudge.

The trouble began in the first simulated session. Daniella had pushed through a budget bill so reckless that even her own backbenchers winced, and Mikhail saw his opening. He stood, announced a motion of no confidence in the chancellor, and called the vote before she could respond. Nicholas, presiding because nobody else wanted the procedural role, hesitated with the gavel halfway raised. Something snagged in his memory, something about Germany being different, and he could not say what.

"That's not how it works there," he said.

"Of course it is. No confidence means no confidence." Mikhail looked at the clock. Rotary at four. "Vote it."

Nicholas lowered the gavel and asked for fifteen minutes, which turned into a frantic search through the reference binders Mr. Costa had carted over from the school library. Daniella followed him to the side table, arms folded, not helping so much as supervising her own potential execution. The binder on the American system gave him one clean counterpoint: a president serves the term the voters gave him, and Congress cannot simply fire him mid-term. That he knew cold. The binder on Germany had a torn index and a coffee ring, and he flipped through it twice before Daniella, reading upside down across from him, jabbed the page with one finger.

"Constructive," she read. "Constructive vote of no confidence."

He read the line twice. The Bundestag can remove a chancellor only by electing a successor in the same vote. He sat back. So you could not simply collapse the government out of spite; you had to name the person you wanted instead, in the very vote that removed the sitting chancellor. Half a minute ago he had assumed all parliaments worked the same way, a prime minister living at the pleasure of the house, and the assumption had calcified so quietly he had never thought to chip at it. He had also assumed, without checking, that Mikhail was wrong. Mikhail was wrong about the outcome but not about the principle of the challenge, and Nicholas had to concede that to himself before he could concede it out loud.

"Okay," he said, walking back to the podium. "The motion fails as written. You can move to remove her, but you have to elect a successor in the same vote. Name someone."

Mikhail stood there with his mouth open, recalculating. Then, instead of naming one of his own allies, which would have been the partisan move, he named Daniella's own finance critic, a quiet girl who had objected to the budget earlier. The government benches went silent. Daniella stared at the name card in front of her and then, visibly, changed her mind about something; she had been planning to storm out if deposed, Nicholas could see it in her shoulders, and instead she stood and defended the budget line by line, honestly, including the parts she now admitted were indefensible. The vote split down the middle and failed by two.

They ran out the clock on a confidence motion that nobody won, and Mr. Costa began stacking chairs at ten to four. Nicholas closed the binders and thought about telling them it was a good exercise, then decided they would hear it better some other day. Mikhail was still at the dispatch table, drawing up another motion, this one with a name already written at the bottom.

"Read it," Mikhail said, and slid it across.
